definitions.definition: 'Director' or 'Additional Director' or 'Joint Director' means a Director or Additional Director or Joint Director, as the case may be, appointed under sub-section (1) of section 49.
definitions.plain_english: An Additional Director is a senior government officer appointed by the Central Government to work under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act. They hold authority just below the Director and above a Joint Director in the enforcement hierarchy. They can exercise powers and perform duties assigned under the Act, including authorising appointment of lower-ranked officers.
real_world_examples: An Additional Director of the Enforcement Directorate in Mumbai oversees investigations into hawala transactions worth hundreds of crores linked to a real estate developer suspected of laundering proceeds from illegal mining.
An Additional Director authorises a Deputy Director to attach properties of an accused in a Punjab drug trafficking case where proceeds were routed through shell companies.

An Additional Director in Delhi exercises powers under PMLA to issue summons to a bank's principal officer seeking records related to suspicious transactions reported by the Financial Intelligence Unit.

An Additional Director at the Enforcement Directorate's Kolkata zonal office supervises investigations into a chit fund fraud where thousands of investors were defrauded and funds were layered through multiple accounts.

An Additional Director, acting under authority delegated by the Director, appoints officers below the rank of Assistant Director to assist in a complex multi-state money laundering investigation involving cryptocurrency exchanges.
what_it_covers: A person appointed by the Central Government specifically under sub-section (1) of section 49 of PMLA to the rank of Additional Director.
An Additional Director who is authorised by the Central Government to appoint other authorities below the rank of Assistant Director.

An Additional Director exercising powers and discharging duties under PMLA subject to conditions and limitations imposed by the Central Government, including investigation of money laundering offences.
Officers of the Enforcement Directorate holding the rank of Additional Director and empowered to act as an authority for purposes of the Act.
what_it_excludes: A Deputy Director, who is a separately defined and lower-ranked authority under section 48 and section 49 of the Act.
An Assistant Director, who is independently defined and holds a rank below Additional Director in the enforcement hierarchy.
Officers holding the title of 'Additional Director' in other government departments or ministries not appointed under sub-section (1) of section 49 of PMLA.
The Director of Enforcement, who is a distinct and higher authority separately referenced in the Act.
Judicial or quasi-judicial authorities such as the Adjudicating Authority or Members of the Appellate Tribunal, who perform adjudicatory rather than investigative/enforcement functions.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as an 'Additional Director' under section 49(1) determines whether their actions — such as authorising attachments, issuing directions, or appointing subordinate officers — carry legal validity under PMLA; any enforcement action taken by a person not properly appointed to this rank could be challenged as without jurisdiction, potentially nullifying proceedings against accused persons.

definitions.definition: 'Adjudicating Authority' means an Adjudicating Authority appointed under sub-section (1) of section 6.
definitions.plain_english: The Adjudicating Authority is a special government-appointed body under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act that decides whether property seized or attached in a money laundering case should be permanently confiscated. It functions like a quasi-judicial tribunal, hearing cases brought by the Enforcement Directorate and giving a fair opportunity to the affected person before making its decision. It is not a regular court but has court-like powers to examine evidence and pass orders on attachment and confiscation of proceeds of crime.
real_world_examples: A Delhi-based real estate developer is accused of laundering money through shell companies. The Enforcement Directorate provisionally attaches his properties worth ₹50 crore under Section 5. The case is then referred to the Adjudicating Authority under Section 8, which holds hearings and decides whether the attachment should be confirmed and the properties confiscated.

A Kolkata hawala operator is found to have transferred funds linked to drug trafficking. After arrest, the Director files a complaint before the Adjudicating Authority, which examines evidence, issues summons to witnesses, and passes an order of confiscation of the bank accounts and cash involved.

A Mumbai-based stockbroker is suspected of layering proceeds from a Ponzi scheme through securities transactions. The Adjudicating Authority reviews the attachment order passed by the Deputy Director and determines whether the attached demat accounts and movable assets constitute proceeds of crime.

Following a bank fraud case in Bengaluru involving a wilful defaulter who siphoned off ₹200 crore, the Adjudicating Authority holds proceedings under Section 8 to adjudicate on the provisional attachment of the accused's overseas properties and domestic assets, ensuring the accused is given a hearing before confirming confiscation.

In a Punjab drug money case, the Adjudicating Authority exercises its powers under Section 11 to summon the principal officer of a chit fund company allegedly used to integrate drug proceeds, examine records, and pass a confiscation order under the PMLA.
what_it_covers: Any authority formally appointed by the Central Government under sub-section (1) of Section 6 of the PMLA to adjudicate matters of attachment and confiscation of proceeds of crime.
A body empowered to confirm, modify or revoke provisional attachment orders made by the Director or Deputy Director under Section 5 of the PMLA.
An authority with quasi-judicial powers to summon persons, examine witnesses, require production of records, and pass orders of confiscation of property involved in money laundering.
The forum before which the Enforcement Directorate files complaints regarding properties suspected to be proceeds of crime, and where the affected person has a right to be heard.
An authority whose orders are subject to appeal before the Appellate Tribunal established under Section 25 of the PMLA.
what_it_excludes: Regular civil courts or criminal courts such as Sessions Courts or High Courts, which are governed by separate provisions and do not perform the adjudication function under Chapter III of the PMLA.

The Appellate Tribunal established under Section 25, which is a separate and higher body that hears appeals against the orders of the Adjudicating Authority and is expressly defined separately in Section 2.

Officers of the Enforcement Directorate such as the Director, Additional Director, Deputy Director, or Assistant Director, who are investigative and enforcement authorities and not adjudicating bodies.

The Special Court designated under Section 43, which handles criminal trials for the offence of money laundering and is distinct from the Adjudicating Authority that handles civil attachment and confiscation proceedings.

Any self-regulatory or departmental authority such as SEBI, RBI, or income tax authorities, even if they exercise quasi-judicial powers in their own domains, as they are not appointed under Section 6(1) of the PMLA.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a body qualifies as the Adjudicating Authority under the PMLA determines the validity of all attachment and confiscation orders passed in money laundering proceedings — only orders from a properly constituted Adjudicating Authority under Section 6(1) carry legal force under Sections 7, 8, and 9, and any person aggrieved has the right to appeal exclusively to the Appellate Tribunal. If the definition is not satisfied, proceedings for confiscation of proceeds of crime can be challenged as without jurisdiction.

definitions.plain_english: The Adjudicating Authority is a special government-appointed body under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act that decides whether property suspected to be proceeds of crime should be formally confiscated. It functions like a quasi-judicial tribunal — it hears cases, examines evidence, and passes orders on attachment and confiscation of assets. It is not a regular court but has powers similar to a civil court for the purposes of this law.
real_world_examples: A Delhi-based real estate developer is accused of laundering money through shell companies. The Enforcement Directorate provisionally attaches his properties and files a complaint before the Adjudicating Authority under Section 8, which then holds proceedings to decide if the attachment should be confirmed and the property confiscated.

A Mumbai hawala operator is arrested and his bank accounts containing alleged proceeds of crime are frozen. The Adjudicating Authority examines the evidence submitted by the Director and determines whether the frozen funds constitute proceeds of crime under Section 20.

A Bengaluru-based software company's accounts are attached on suspicion of laundering money through fictitious export invoices. The Adjudicating Authority conducts hearings under Section 8, reviews financial records, and passes a final confiscation order after giving the accused an opportunity to be heard.

A politician in Hyderabad is found to own agricultural land allegedly purchased using bribe money linked to a scheduled offence. The Adjudicating Authority receives the complaint from the Enforcement Directorate and decides whether to confirm the provisional attachment of the land under Chapter III.

A Chennai-based jewellery trader is suspected of converting drug money into gold. After provisional attachment, the Adjudicating Authority under Section 21 takes custody of the seized records and documents produced before it to aid its adjudication process.

The authority that manages custody and records of attached properties under Sections 20 and 21, including documents and assets seized during investigation.
The forum before which a person whose property is attached can appear, present evidence, and contest confiscation proceedings under the Act.

Its jurisdiction directly triggers the confiscation consequence under Section 8 and governs the custodial obligations over attached property under Sections 20 and 21.

definitions.definition: Adjudication refers to the formal quasi-judicial process conducted by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 8 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, whereby, upon receipt of a complaint or application, it examines whether properties attached or seized are involved in money-laundering, hears the concerned parties, and passes an order confirming attachment, retention, or confiscation of such properties. It encompasses the entire proceeding from issuance of notice to the final order of confiscation after the guilt of the person is established by a trial court.
definitions.plain_english: Adjudication is the official legal process where a government-appointed authority (the Adjudicating Authority) decides whether money or property seized from a person was actually obtained through money laundering. The authority sends a notice to the person asking them to explain where their money came from, listens to both sides, reviews evidence, and then either confirms that the property is linked to money laundering or releases it. If money laundering is proven in court, the property can be permanently taken away by the government.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based real estate developer is found to have purchased multiple properties using proceeds from hawala transactions. The Enforcement Directorate attaches these properties under Section 5 and files a complaint before the Adjudicating Authority. The Authority issues a 30-day notice asking the developer to explain the source of funds; after hearing both sides, it confirms the attachment and eventually orders confiscation after the special court convicts the developer.

A Delhi-based shell company director has her bank accounts and assets seized under Section 17 during a search. The authorised officer retains the property for adjudication under Section 8 and forwards materials to the Adjudicating Authority. After adjudication proceedings, the Authority finds the assets are prima facie involved in money laundering and permits retention beyond the initial three-month period.

A Kolkata jeweller is suspected of layering illicit funds through multiple jewellery purchases. After provisional attachment, the Adjudicating Authority conducts adjudication, hears the jeweller's representative and the Director's officer, and passes a written order confirming that the jewellery stock is involved in money laundering, directing the Enforcement Directorate to take possession.

A Hyderabad-based politician's relative holds properties allegedly purchased with bribe proceeds. The Adjudicating Authority issues notice not only to the relative but also to the politician, as the property is held on behalf of another person. During adjudication, a third-party claimant also gets an opportunity to prove their innocent title before a final confiscation order is passed.

A Chennai-based non-banking financial company officer is acquitted by the Special Court of the underlying scheduled offence. Following the acquittal, the adjudication proceedings result in the cessation of the attachment, and all retained property and net income are returned to the officer, demonstrating how adjudication outcomes are tied to trial court results.
what_it_covers: The formal process of issuing a notice of not less than thirty days to a person calling upon them to explain the source of income or assets used to acquire attached or seized property.

The hearing and consideration of replies, evidence, and oral submissions from the aggrieved person and the Director or authorised officer before passing a finding on whether property is involved in money laundering.

Passing a written order confirming the attachment of property made under Section 5(1) or retention of property/records seized under Sections 17 or 18, and eventual confiscation after the trial court's guilt finding becomes final.
Proceedings involving third parties who hold property on behalf of another person or jointly hold such property, including giving them notice and an opportunity to be heard.

Review and authorisation of retention of seized property or records beyond the initial three-month period where the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied the property is prima facie involved in money laundering.
what_it_excludes: Criminal trial proceedings before the Special Court for conviction of the scheduled offence, which is a separate judicial process and a prerequisite for making confiscation final under adjudication.

The initial search, survey, seizure, or provisional attachment actions undertaken by the Enforcement Directorate under Sections 5, 17, or 18, which precede and trigger adjudication but are not part of it.
Appellate proceedings before the Appellate Tribunal under Section 26, which constitute a separate review mechanism after the adjudication order is passed.
Civil court proceedings or proceedings before any other judicial forum concerning the same property, since adjudication is exclusively vested in the Adjudicating Authority under PMLA.
Administrative or investigative steps such as summons, survey, or information gathering by investigating officers, which are pre-adjudication enforcement actions.
definitions.why_it_matters: Adjudication is the pivotal process that determines whether provisionally attached or seized property is legally confirmed as involved in money laundering, directly triggering the government's right to take possession and ultimately confiscate such property under Section 8(4) and (6). Without a valid adjudication order confirming attachment, the provisional attachment lapses, the property must be returned, and the entire enforcement action under the PMLA against the accused person fails.

definitions.definition: An Administrator is an officer of the Central Government, not below the rank of a Joint Secretary to the Government of India, appointed by order published in the Official Gazette under sub-section (1) of section 10, to receive and manage properties in relation to which an order has been made under sub-section (6) of section 8, and to dispose of property vested in the Central Government under section 9, in such manner and subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.
definitions.plain_english: An Administrator is a senior government official (at least at the level of a Joint Secretary) officially appointed by the Central Government to take charge of and manage properties that have been attached or confiscated under the money laundering law. Think of them as a court-appointed property manager who looks after seized assets — such as land, buildings, or businesses — on behalf of the government until they are officially disposed of. They can also apply to courts to help recover property suspected to be located in foreign countries.
real_world_examples: A Joint Secretary-level IAS officer is appointed as Administrator to manage a luxury hotel in Mumbai that has been confiscated from a real estate developer convicted of money laundering, ensuring the hotel continues to operate and generate revenue for the government during the disposal process.

After the Enforcement Directorate attaches multiple agricultural land parcels in Punjab allegedly purchased with proceeds of a drug trafficking syndicate, an Administrator is appointed to prevent encroachment, collect rents, and maintain records of the properties until the Adjudicating Authority's final order is executed.

An Administrator appointed under Section 10 files an application before the Special Court in Delhi requesting a letter of request to be sent to the United Arab Emirates, where a accused's offshore villa — suspected to be bought with laundered funds — is believed to be located, so that the property can be attached in the contracting State.

Following confiscation of a chain of gold jewellery shops in Chennai belonging to a hawala operator, the Central Government appoints an Administrator who takes over the shops, manages inventory, oversees staff, and arranges for the orderly auctioning of assets as directed by the Central Government under Section 10(3).

In a bank fraud case involving a shell company in Kolkata, the Administrator is directed by the Central Government to liquidate attached commercial office spaces and deposit the proceeds into the government treasury, coordinating with valuers and legal teams to ensure compliance with prescribed conditions.
what_it_covers: A Joint Secretary-level or higher Central Government officer formally appointed via an Official Gazette notification to manage confiscated or attached properties under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act.

Management and preservation of any property — movable or immovable — in respect of which an order under sub-section (6) of section 8 has been passed by the Adjudicating Authority, including day-to-day operations of businesses or estates.
Disposal of property that has been vested in the Central Government under section 9, including arranging auctions, sales, or transfers as directed by the Central Government.

Filing of applications before the Special Court for the issuance of letters of request to courts or authorities in contracting States to facilitate attachment or confiscation of property located abroad.
what_it_excludes: Officers below the rank of Joint Secretary to the Government of India, who cannot be appointed as Administrator regardless of their seniority within their own department or cadre.

Private individuals, liquidators, official receivers, or court-appointed receivers under other laws (such as the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code) — they do not qualify as an Administrator under this Act even if managing similar assets.

The Adjudicating Authority or the Director of the Enforcement Directorate, who have separate and distinct statutory roles under the Act and are not empowered to perform the functions of the Administrator.
State Government officers or officials of autonomous bodies who have not been specifically appointed by the Central Government through the required Official Gazette order.
definitions.why_it_matters: The appointment of an Administrator is the legal mechanism that ensures confiscated and attached properties do not fall into disuse, lose value, or remain unmanaged during the period between attachment and final disposal — protecting the economic interest of the State. The Administrator's standing to apply before the Special Court (under Section 60) also directly enables international cooperation for cross-border asset recovery, making this role pivotal in cases where proceeds of crime have been moved to contracting States.

definitions.definition: 'Assistant Director' means an Assistant Director appointed under sub-section (1) of section 49.
definitions.plain_english: An Assistant Director is a government officer formally appointed under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act to assist in enforcing the law. This officer has specific powers granted by the Act, including the authority to arrest persons suspected of money laundering offences. The Assistant Director works within the enforcement hierarchy established under the Act.
real_world_examples: An Assistant Director of the Enforcement Directorate in Mumbai, appointed under Section 49, records reasons in writing and arrests a hawala operator suspected of laundering proceeds from drug trafficking through shell companies.

An Assistant Director posted at the ED's Delhi Zonal Office conducts a search of a real estate firm's premises after receiving intelligence about layering of funds obtained through corruption, exercising powers granted under the Act.

An Assistant Director in Chennai, on the basis of Suspicious Transaction Reports received from a bank, arrests a businessman who is found to have routed proceeds of crime through multiple benami accounts across several states.

An Assistant Director in Kolkata forwards a sealed copy of the arrest order along with supporting material to the Adjudicating Authority immediately after arresting a person accused of laundering money generated from cyber fraud operations.

An Assistant Director operating under a Central Government special order in Hyderabad exercises arrest powers against a person suspected of laundering funds derived from illegal mining operations, and produces the arrested person before a Judicial Magistrate within twenty-four hours.
what_it_covers: An officer formally appointed under sub-section (1) of Section 49 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act by the Central Government as an Assistant Director.
An Assistant Director who possesses material-based reasonable belief and exercises the power to arrest a person suspected of committing a scheduled money laundering offence under Section 19.

An Assistant Director who is required to forward a sealed copy of the arrest order and supporting material to the Adjudicating Authority immediately after making an arrest, as prescribed under Section 19.
An Assistant Director authorised to act within the enforcement structure established under Section 49 alongside the Director, Additional Director, Joint Director, and Deputy Director.
what_it_excludes: Officers from other central or state government agencies (e.g., CBI, Income Tax Department, Police) who are not specifically appointed under sub-section (1) of Section 49 of the PMLA.
A Deputy Director, Joint Director, Additional Director, or Director, as these are separately defined positions within the same enforcement hierarchy under Section 49.
Any private individual, contractor, or outsourced investigator engaged by the government but not formally appointed through the statutory mechanism under Section 49(1).
Officers appointed under other Central Government Acts (such as FEMA or Customs Act) who have not been given a concurrent appointment or authorisation under PMLA Section 49.

definitions.definition: 'Attachment' means prohibition of transfer, conversion, disposition or movement of property by an order issued under Chapter III.
definitions.plain_english: Attachment means a legal freeze placed on a person's property so that it cannot be sold, moved, converted into another form, or otherwise dealt with. This freeze is imposed by an official order under the money laundering law. The property remains in the owner's possession but is effectively locked until further legal proceedings determine its fate.
real_world_examples: A Delhi-based hawala operator is found to have routed crores of rupees through shell companies. The Deputy Director of the Enforcement Directorate issues a provisional attachment order freezing all bank accounts, land parcels, and vehicles registered in the operator's name pending confiscation proceedings.

A Mumbai real estate developer is accused of laundering proceeds from drug trafficking by investing in luxury apartments. The Enforcement Directorate attaches the completed flats and under-construction units, prohibiting the developer from selling, mortgaging, or transferring them to any third party.

A Bengaluru-based fintech company's directors are arrested for allegedly laundering funds through fictitious loan repayments. The Adjudicating Authority confirms attachment of the company's office premises and digital assets, preventing their conversion or disposal during trial.

A Kolkata gold trader is suspected of converting proceeds of a scheduled fraud offence into gold bars and jewellery. The Director of Enforcement attaches the gold inventory stored in bank lockers and the trader's warehouse, blocking any movement or transfer of the attached goods.

A Hyderabad politician's family trust is linked to disproportionate assets arising from alleged corruption. The Enforcement Directorate attaches agricultural land, commercial plots, and fixed deposits held by the trust, freezing all disposition pending adjudication before the Adjudicating Authority.
what_it_covers: Bank accounts and fixed deposits provisionally frozen by an Enforcement Directorate order to prevent fund transfers linked to money laundering.
Immovable property such as land, residential flats, and commercial premises prohibited from being sold, gifted, or mortgaged under a Chapter III order.
Movable assets including vehicles, gold, jewellery, and shares whose conversion, disposal, or movement is prohibited by an attachment order.
Intangible property such as intellectual property rights or digital assets whose disposition or transfer is blocked pursuant to an order under Chapter III.
Property held by third parties in a benami capacity where the beneficial interest is traced back to proceeds of crime and restrained by an attachment order.
what_it_excludes: Seizure or physical taking of property by enforcement authorities, which involves actual dispossession rather than mere prohibition of transfer or movement.
Court-ordered attachment under the Code of Civil Procedure for the recovery of civil debts, which is not issued under Chapter III of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act.
Confiscation of property, which is the final vesting of title in the Central Government after adjudication, as opposed to the interim prohibition constituting attachment.
Voluntary undertakings or contractual restrictions on property transfer agreed between private parties, which do not arise from a statutory order under Chapter III.
Arrest or detention of a person accused of money laundering, which is a restraint on personal liberty and is distinct from attachment of property.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a restraint on property qualifies as 'attachment' under this Act determines whether the rigorous procedural safeguards, timelines, and adjudication mechanisms of Chapter III apply, including the requirement of confirmation by the Adjudicating Authority within the prescribed period. Attachment is the foundational trigger for confiscation proceedings under Section 8, and its validity directly affects the rights of the property owner to challenge the order before the Appellate Tribunal.

definitions.plain_english: The term 'authorities' refers to the designated government officials empowered to enforce the anti-money laundering law in India. These include senior officers like the Director, Additional Director, and Joint Director, down to Deputy Directors and Assistant Directors, as well as any other officers the government may appoint. These are the people who can investigate, attach property, and take action against money laundering.
real_world_examples: An Assistant Director posted at the Enforcement Directorate office in Mumbai receives a suspicious transaction report and initiates an inquiry into a shell company suspected of laundering hawala money.

A Deputy Director of the Enforcement Directorate issues a summons to a Kolkata-based jeweller suspected of converting proceeds from illegal mining into gold purchases, exercising powers conferred on 'authorities' under the Act.

A Joint Director oversees and approves a provisional attachment order against bank accounts and immovable property of a real estate developer in Bengaluru, where the property is suspected to be proceeds of crime from a bank fraud.

The Director of Enforcement, acting as the head authority, issues a letter of request to a foreign jurisdiction seeking information about overseas assets held by an accused person under investigation for laundering funds obtained through corruption in a public procurement scam.

An Additional Director authorises a search and seizure operation at the premises of a Hyderabad-based fintech company suspected of being used as a conduit for layering proceeds from cybercrime, exercising survey and search powers vested in authorities under the Act.

Courts, including Special Courts and the High Court, which exercise judicial powers under the Act and are not administrative or enforcement authorities under Section 48.
Police officers investigating scheduled offences under other laws, unless specifically appointed as officers under Section 48 for PMLA purposes.

definitions.plain_english: An 'authority' under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act refers to any official or body that has been given legal power to carry out investigations, conduct searches, issue directions, or take enforcement actions related to money laundering. Essentially, it means any person or body legally authorised to implement or enforce the provisions of this Act.
real_world_examples: The Director of the Enforcement Directorate (ED) conducting a survey under Section 16 at the premises of a hawala operator in Mumbai suspected of laundering proceeds from drug trafficking.
A Deputy Director authorised by the ED Director issuing a provisional attachment order under Section 5 against immovable properties of a Kolkata-based businessman linked to a scheduled fraud offence.
An Assistant Director, acting as an 'authority' under Section 63, recording statements from bank officials of a nationalised bank in Delhi suspected of facilitating layering of illicit funds.

The Central Government designating officers of the Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-IND) as an 'authority' under Section 52 to share financial intelligence and coordinate with foreign agencies in a cross-border money laundering investigation involving shell companies in the GIFT City, Gujarat.

Any officer or body specifically authorised by the Central Government under Section 52 or 53 to exercise powers of investigation, inspection, or information gathering.
Officers empowered to conduct surveys under Section 16, including entering premises, examining records, and collecting evidence related to money laundering.

Officers exercising powers under Section 63 to record statements and gather evidence that may be used in adjudication or prosecution proceedings.
what_it_excludes: The Adjudicating Authority, which is a separate body appointed under Section 6 with distinct quasi-judicial functions and is expressly defined separately in Section 2.

definitions.plain_english: Banking companies are simply banks that are legally incorporated as companies and operate banking business in India under the Banking Regulation Act. In the context of this law, they are treated as key gatekeepers responsible for detecting and reporting suspicious or large financial transactions to help prevent money laundering. They must keep detailed records of their customers and transactions and share relevant information with the government authority whenever required.
real_world_examples: State Bank of India, being a banking company operating in India, is required under PMLA to maintain records of all cash transactions above Rs. 10 lakh and report suspicious transactions to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-IND) within the prescribed time.

HDFC Bank Ltd., a private sector banking company, must conduct Know Your Customer (KYC) verification for all account holders and maintain those identity records for at least ten years after the customer relationship ends, as mandated by Section 12 of the PMLA.

Punjab National Bank detected a series of structured transactions by a customer, each just below the prescribed threshold, designed to avoid reporting. As a banking company under PMLA, its principal officer was obligated to report these transactions to the Director despite them individually falling below the prescribed value.

ICICI Bank, while processing a large wire transfer to a foreign account, identified the transaction as potentially linked to proceeds of crime. As a banking company under PMLA, it was required to file a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) with FIU-IND and could not be held civilly liable for doing so, as protected under Section 14.

Axis Bank, during a routine audit, discovered that a corporate client had been routing funds through multiple accounts to obscure their origin. Being a banking company under PMLA, Axis Bank's compliance team was required to freeze cooperation with the client and report the pattern to the enforcement authorities.

Small Finance Banks and Payments Banks incorporated as companies and licensed by the Reserve Bank of India under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
Regional Rural Banks incorporated as companies under applicable statutes and engaged in banking operations subject to PMLA obligations.

Chit fund companies, which are separately defined and categorised under PMLA and do not fall within the 'banking companies' category even if they deal in financial transactions.
Housing finance institutions regulated by the National Housing Bank, which are separately defined under PMLA and are not classified as banking companies.

definitions.plain_english: A 'Bench' refers to a sitting or panel of one or more members of the Appellate Tribunal who are assigned to hear and decide a particular appeal or matter under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act. It is the functional unit through which the Appellate Tribunal exercises its judicial powers. Different Benches may be constituted to handle different cases simultaneously.
real_world_examples: When a person whose property has been attached under PMLA files an appeal against the Adjudicating Authority's order, the Chairperson of the Appellate Tribunal constitutes a Bench of two Members to hear and decide the appeal in New Delhi.

The Appellate Tribunal in Mumbai constitutes a special Bench comprising the Chairperson and one Member to urgently hear an appeal filed by a real estate developer challenging an order of attachment worth ₹500 crore linked to a money laundering case.

A bank aggrieved by an order passed by the Adjudicating Authority under PMLA files an appeal, and the Chairperson assigns the matter to a Single-Member Bench for preliminary hearing on whether the appeal is maintainable.

In a high-profile hawala case involving multiple accused, the Appellate Tribunal constitutes separate Benches to simultaneously hear the individual appeals filed by different appellants so as to expedite proceedings.

A Bench of the Appellate Tribunal sitting at Chennai hears an appeal by a chit fund company contesting the confiscation of its assets that were alleged to be proceeds of a scheduled offence under PMLA.
what_it_covers: A panel comprising the Chairperson alone or with one or more Members of the Appellate Tribunal constituted to hear an appeal under PMLA.
A Bench constituted by the Chairperson of the Appellate Tribunal specifically for deciding appeals arising from orders of the Adjudicating Authority.
A Division Bench or Single-Member Bench of the Appellate Tribunal exercising powers under Sections 36, 37, and 38 of PMLA to admit, hear, and dispose of appeals.
Any sitting of the Appellate Tribunal, whether at its principal seat or a circuit bench, constituted in accordance with the rules governing the Tribunal's functioning under PMLA.
what_it_excludes: A Bench of the Adjudicating Authority constituted under Section 6 of PMLA — that is a separate body and not the 'Bench' as defined under Section 2.
Benches of other tribunals, courts, or statutory bodies such as the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal or the Debt Recovery Tribunal, even if they deal with related financial matters.
A single officer of the Enforcement Directorate or any investigating authority conducting proceedings — these are not judicial benches of the Appellate Tribunal.
The Special Court designated under Section 43 of PMLA, which is a criminal court and not a Bench of the Appellate Tribunal.
definitions.why_it_matters: The constitution and jurisdiction of a 'Bench' determines the validity of appellate proceedings under Sections 36, 37, and 38 of PMLA — an order passed by a wrongly constituted or unauthorised Bench may be void and unenforceable. It directly governs which forum has authority to grant stays, hear appeals, and pass binding orders on attachment and confiscation matters.

definitions.definition: The term 'Central Government' is not expressly defined in the Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002, but as used throughout the Act, it refers to the Union Government of India, acting through the Ministry of Finance or such other Ministry as may be authorised, which exercises executive, regulatory, and administrative powers conferred by this Act, including the power to appoint authorities, issue notifications, frame rules, and take policy decisions necessary for implementation of the Act.
definitions.plain_english: The Central Government means the Government of India, typically acting through the Ministry of Finance. It is the highest executive authority responsible for putting this law into effect, appointing key officials, and making rules under it. Think of it as the national government in New Delhi that oversees how this anti-money laundering law is enforced across the whole country.
real_world_examples: The Ministry of Finance, on behalf of the Central Government, issues a notification in the Official Gazette appointing a new Adjudicating Authority to hear money laundering cases under Section 6 of the Act.
The Central Government exercises its power under Section 32 to remove a Member of the Appellate Tribunal from office after conducting an inquiry into allegations of misconduct against that Member.

The Central Government frames and notifies rules under the PMLA prescribing the procedure for attachment and confiscation of properties, which the Enforcement Directorate then follows during investigations.

Pursuant to its powers under the Act, the Central Government appoints the Director of the Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-IND) and the Director of the Enforcement Directorate as authorities for the purposes of the Act.

The Central Government, in response to international FATF recommendations, amends the Schedule to the PMLA by adding new predicate offences, thereby expanding the scope of scheduled offences in India.

The Central Government enters into agreements with contracting States for mutual legal assistance in money laundering investigations and notifies such arrangements in the Official Gazette under the Act.
what_it_covers: The Union Government of India acting through the Ministry of Finance in all matters pertaining to the PMLA.
Any Ministry or Department of the Government of India that is authorised or notified to exercise specific powers under the Act.
Actions taken by duly authorised officers or bodies acting under the direction and on behalf of the Union Executive in furtherance of the Act's provisions.
The executive power exercised through official notifications in the Official Gazette appointing authorities, specifying dates of commencement, or framing rules.
The power to remove or suspend Members of the Appellate Tribunal and Adjudicating Authority as contemplated under Section 32.
what_it_excludes: State Governments of individual Indian states, which are distinct constitutional entities and do not exercise powers reserved for the Central Government under the PMLA.
The Judiciary, including the Supreme Court, High Courts, Special Courts, and the Appellate Tribunal, which are independent constitutional or statutory bodies and not part of the Central Government.

Autonomous statutory bodies such as the Reserve Bank of India, SEBI, or IRDAI, even when they exercise regulatory functions related to money laundering compliance, as they are not the Central Government.
Local self-governing bodies such as Municipal Corporations, Panchayats, or District Authorities, which have no role as 'Central Government' under the Act.
Foreign governments or international organisations, even those cooperating with India on anti-money laundering matters under mutual legal assistance treaties.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identity of the Central Government as the empowered authority under the PMLA is critical because actions such as appointment of the Adjudicating Authority, establishment of the Appellate Tribunal, issuance of binding notifications, and removal of Members under Section 32 derive their legal validity only when performed by the Central Government; any such action by an unauthorised body would be void and without legal effect, potentially invalidating prosecutions, attachments, or confiscations that flow from those appointments.

definitions.definition: 'Chairperson' means the Chairperson of the Appellate Tribunal.
definitions.plain_english: The Chairperson is the head or presiding officer of the Appellate Tribunal established under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act. This is the senior-most judicial or quasi-judicial authority within the Appellate Tribunal who oversees its functioning, constitutes Benches, and ensures the tribunal operates effectively. The Chairperson also holds the status of a Member of the Appellate Tribunal.
real_world_examples: A retired High Court Judge is appointed by the Central Government as the Chairperson of the Appellate Tribunal under PMLA and presides over appeals filed by persons aggrieved by orders of the Adjudicating Authority attaching properties worth crores of rupees linked to hawala transactions.

The Chairperson of the Appellate Tribunal constitutes a special Bench of two Members to hear an urgent appeal from a Mumbai-based real estate developer whose properties were provisionally attached by the Enforcement Directorate in connection with a money laundering case.

When the post of Chairperson falls vacant due to retirement, the Central Government makes a temporary arrangement under Section 30 to ensure the Appellate Tribunal continues to hear pending appeals from accused persons contesting attachment orders.

The Chairperson exercises administrative powers under Section 37 to regulate the practice and procedure of the Appellate Tribunal, issuing directions on filing of appeals, hearing schedules, and submission of documents in a high-profile bank fraud money laundering case involving multiple accused.

A litigant files a complaint under Section 36 regarding the conduct of a Member of the Appellate Tribunal; the matter is placed before the Chairperson who initiates the appropriate inquiry as prescribed under the Act.

The Chairperson of the Appellate Tribunal presides over a Bench that hears an appeal by a non-banking financial company aggrieved by the Adjudicating Authority's order confirming attachment of its assets in a Ponzi scheme money laundering investigation.
what_it_covers: The presiding head of the Appellate Tribunal established under Section 25 of the PMLA who is appointed by the Central Government.
A person who simultaneously holds the status of 'Member' of the Appellate Tribunal by virtue of being the Chairperson, as expressly provided in the definition of 'Member' under Section 2.
The officer empowered to constitute Benches of the Appellate Tribunal and assign Members to hear specific appeals or cases under PMLA.

The authority responsible for the administrative and procedural functioning of the Appellate Tribunal, including matters under Sections 36, 37, and 38 relating to procedure, staff, and tribunal conduct.
The person with respect to whom special provisions regarding vacancy, resignation, and removal apply under Sections 30 and 31 of the Act.
what_it_excludes: The Chairperson of an Adjudicating Authority appointed under Section 6, who is a distinct officer heading the Adjudicating Authority and not the Appellate Tribunal.
Any Member of the Appellate Tribunal who is not specifically designated as Chairperson, even if acting in a senior capacity.

Officers of the Enforcement Directorate such as the Director, Additional Director, Joint Director, Deputy Director, or Assistant Director, who are investigative and enforcement authorities, not tribunal heads.
The Presiding Officer or judge of a Special Court designated under Section 43, who exercises criminal jurisdiction and is not part of the Appellate Tribunal structure.

Any authority functioning under a different legislation (such as the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal Chairperson or FEMA Appellate Tribunal head) even if performing similar functions in related subject matters.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identity and authority of the Chairperson directly determines the valid constitution of Benches and the lawful conduct of appellate proceedings under PMLA — any order passed by an improperly constituted Bench or in the absence of a validly appointed Chairperson may be legally challenged. Provisions governing the Chairperson's appointment, tenure, resignation, and removal under Sections 30 and 31 ensure institutional independence and continuity, which is critical to the fair adjudication of attachment and confiscation orders affecting individuals and entities accused of money laundering.

definitions.definition: "chit fund company" means a company managing, conducting or supervising, as foreman, agent or in any other capacity, chits as defined in section 2 of the Chit Funds Act, 1982 (40 of 1982).
definitions.plain_english: A chit fund company is a business entity that organises and runs chit fund schemes, where a group of people contribute money periodically into a common pool, and members take turns receiving the pooled amount. The company acts as the manager or organiser of these rotating savings arrangements. Under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, such companies are treated as financial institutions and must follow anti-money laundering rules.
real_world_examples: A registered company in Kerala operating Kuri schemes where 50 members each contribute ₹10,000 monthly and one member receives the pot each month through auction or lot — such a company is a chit fund company under PMLA.

A Tamil Nadu-based company like Shriram Chits conducting prize chit schemes across multiple branches, acting as foreman collecting subscriptions and disbursing amounts to subscribers, falls within this definition and must register with FIU-IND.

An Andhra Pradesh incorporated entity managing chit schemes for gold jewellers, supervising monthly auctions and maintaining subscriber records, qualifies as a chit fund company and is subject to PMLA reporting obligations.

A Delhi-registered company acting as an agent for a large chit fund operator, collecting instalments from subscribers and remitting them to the foreman entity, is covered under this definition due to its agency capacity.

A company in Telangana running an online digital chit fund platform where subscribers bid electronically and the company acts as foreman managing the entire scheme is a chit fund company subject to know-your-customer (KYC) and suspicious transaction reporting norms under PMLA.
what_it_covers: A company acting as foreman that directly organises and conducts chit schemes by collecting periodic subscriptions from a group of subscribers and disbursing the prize amount.
A company supervising chit schemes in an agency capacity on behalf of another party, including digital or online platforms managing the scheme operations.
A company incorporated under the Companies Act that manages multiple simultaneous chit groups across different geographies, irrespective of ticket size or subscriber count.
Any entity qualifying as a 'company' that administers chits as defined under section 2 of the Chit Funds Act, 1982, regardless of whether it operates under a state government licence.
A company acting in 'any other capacity' in relation to chit management, including administrative, supervisory, or coordination roles integral to running the chit scheme.
what_it_excludes: Individuals or Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs) running informal neighbourhood chit arrangements, as they do not constitute a 'company' within the corporate legal sense.
Partnership firms or unincorporated associations conducting chit-like schemes, since the definition is restricted to companies and does not extend to non-corporate entities.
Non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) and housing finance institutions that do not manage chits, even though they are separately classified as financial institutions under the same Act.
State governments or government-owned entities running savings schemes that resemble chits but are not structured as chits under the Chit Funds Act, 1982.
Banks and co-operative banks, which are separately defined under PMLA and whose recurring deposit or group savings products do not constitute chits under the Chit Funds Act, 1982.
definitions.why_it_matters: A chit fund company is expressly included within the definition of 'financial institution' under PMLA, which means it is subject to the full suite of anti-money laundering obligations including client due diligence, maintenance of records, and reporting of suspicious transactions to the Financial Intelligence Unit — failure to comply can attract prosecution and attachment of proceeds of crime. Whether an entity qualifies as a chit fund company determines whether PMLA's preventive and enforcement provisions, including obligations under Chapter IV, apply to it.

definitions.definition: A civil court under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 refers to a court exercising civil jurisdiction under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, whose powers are vested in or exercisable by the Adjudicating Authority, the Director, and the Appellate Tribunal for specified purposes under this Act. definitions.definition: 'co-operative bank' shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in clause (dd) of section 2 of the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation Act, 1961 (47 of 1961).
definitions.plain_english: A co-operative bank is a type of bank that is organized and run on co-operative principles, meaning it is owned and managed by its members for their mutual benefit. These banks are registered under co-operative society laws and also regulated under the Banking Regulation Act. They serve specific communities, regions, or occupational groups and accept deposits and provide loans to their members.
real_world_examples: The Saraswat Co-operative Bank Limited in Mumbai accepting fixed deposits from members — it qualifies as a co-operative bank and is therefore subject to PMLA reporting obligations for suspicious transactions.

A district central co-operative bank in rural Maharashtra facilitating large cash transactions for agricultural loans — such transactions must be monitored and reported under PMLA anti-money laundering norms.

An urban co-operative bank in Gujarat through which a real estate developer routes proceeds from illegal land deals — the bank is treated as a 'financial institution' under PMLA and its officers can be held liable for failing to report suspicious activity.

The Cosmos Co-operative Bank in Pune being used by shell entities to transfer funds linked to a scheduled offence — since it is a co-operative bank and thus a financial institution under PMLA, it falls within the jurisdiction of the Enforcement Directorate for investigation.

A primary agricultural credit society (PACS) that does not fall under the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation Act, 1961 — it would not qualify as a co-operative bank for PMLA purposes, illustrating the boundary of the definition.
what_it_covers: Urban co-operative banks registered under state co-operative societies laws and regulated under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, such as Saraswat Bank or Cosmos Bank.
State co-operative banks and district central co-operative banks that are covered under clause (dd) of section 2 of the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation Act, 1961.
Multi-state co-operative banks operating across state boundaries that are registered under the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002 and fall within the DICGC Act's definition.
Co-operative banks that accept deposits from the public and are therefore insured by the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation, making them squarely within the PMLA definition.
what_it_excludes: Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) that are not classified as co-operative banks under clause (dd) of section 2 of the DICGC Act, 1961.
Non-banking co-operative societies engaged only in lending among members without holding a banking licence or being covered by the DICGC Act.
Scheduled commercial banks (such as State Bank of India or HDFC Bank) which are separately covered as 'banking companies' under the Act and are not co-operative in structure.
Microfinance institutions or self-help group federations that operate on co-operative-like principles but are not registered or regulated as co-operative banks under applicable banking laws.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a 'co-operative bank' determines whether it is classified as a 'financial institution' under PMLA, thereby triggering mandatory obligations to maintain records, verify client identity, and report suspicious transactions to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-IND). Failure to comply with these obligations can expose the bank and its principal officers to prosecution for the offence of money-laundering or related contraventions under the Act.

definitions.definition: The term 'company' is not separately defined in Section 2 of this Act, but as used in the Act, 'company' means a company as defined under the Companies Act, and is expressly included as a sub-category of 'person' under Section 2 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. For the purposes of Section 70, a company means any body corporate incorporated under any law for the time being in force, including its directors, managers, secretaries, and other officers who are responsible for the conduct of its business.
definitions.plain_english: A 'company' refers to a business entity that has been legally registered and incorporated under company law, such as a private limited company or a public limited company in India. It is treated as a separate legal person under this Act, which means a company itself can commit money laundering offences. When a company is found guilty, the individual officers such as directors and managers who were responsible for running the company can also be held personally liable.
real_world_examples: A Bengaluru-based private limited company is used as a shell entity to layer and integrate proceeds from a drug trafficking network by routing funds through fake invoices and inter-company loans — the company itself, along with its managing director, can be prosecuted under the PMLA.

A Mumbai-listed public company's CFO routes kickbacks received from government contracts through the company's overseas subsidiaries to disguise their criminal origin — both the company as an entity and the CFO can be held liable under Section 70 of the PMLA.

A real estate company in Delhi systematically accepts large cash payments for property transactions without reporting them as required, thereby facilitating money laundering — the company and its promoters are subject to attachment of proceeds of crime and prosecution.

A chit fund company registered in Kolkata collects illegal deposits from the public and funnels those funds through a web of affiliated companies to conceal the criminal proceeds — all constituent companies involved and their officers face liability under the PMLA.

A non-banking financial company (NBFC) registered in Chennai is found to have knowingly disbursed loans against proceeds of crime presented as legitimate collateral — both the NBFC as a company and its principal officers are liable to prosecution and attachment of property under the Act.
what_it_covers: Private limited companies incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 or earlier Companies Acts, including shell companies and holding companies used for layering criminal proceeds.
Public limited companies listed or unlisted, including their directors, managers, company secretaries, and other officers who are in charge of the company's business operations.
Foreign companies operating in India that are registered or conducting business within Indian jurisdiction, insofar as their activities trigger money laundering offences under this Act.
Any body corporate constituted under a special statute (e.g., a public sector undertaking formed by an Act of Parliament) where the context of money laundering applies.
One-person companies and small companies incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, when involved in transactions constituting money laundering.
what_it_excludes: Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs), which are separately listed as a distinct sub-category of 'person' under Section 2 and are not treated as companies.

Partnerships and firms registered under the Partnership Act, 1932 or LLPs under the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, which are separately categorised as 'firm' under the definition of 'person'.
Unincorporated associations or bodies of individuals, which are covered under a separate sub-clause of the definition of 'person' and do not qualify as 'company'.
Individual natural persons and sole proprietorships, which are covered under the 'individual' sub-category of 'person' and not under 'company'.
Government departments and ministries acting in a sovereign capacity, which are generally not treated as companies for the purposes of corporate criminal liability under this Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a 'company' directly determines the applicability of Section 70 of the PMLA, which enables simultaneous prosecution of both the company and its officers-in-charge (such as directors and managers) for money laundering offences, thereby triggering personal criminal liability for individuals beyond just the corporate entity. This classification also determines which reporting obligations, attachment proceedings, and confiscation orders apply to the entity and its assets under the Act.

definitions.definition: Confiscation refers to the permanent transfer of title and ownership of property involved in money-laundering to the Central Government by an order made under sub-section (6) of section 8 of the Act, whereby all rights and title in such property vest absolutely in the Central Government free from all encumbrances, following adjudication by the Adjudicating Authority.
definitions.plain_english: Confiscation means the government permanently takes away property that was found to be connected to money-laundering. Once confiscated, the property fully belongs to the Central Government and no prior loans, mortgages, or claims on the property remain valid. This is different from a temporary freeze or seizure — confiscation is the final, permanent step.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based hawala operator's three residential flats in Andheri and a commercial plot in Pune, traced as proceeds of a ₹50 crore illegal fund transfer network, are permanently confiscated by the Central Government after the Adjudicating Authority passes an order under Section 8(6).

A Delhi politician found guilty of laundering bribery proceeds through shell companies has his luxury car fleet and foreign currency deposits confiscated following a PMLA adjudication, with all vehicle registration titles vesting in the Central Government.

A Bengaluru-based drug trafficking syndicate's proceeds, including a farmhouse in Hosur and fixed deposits in a private bank, are confiscated after the Adjudicating Authority confirms they constitute proceeds of crime under a scheduled narcotic offence.

A Kolkata jeweller who laundered proceeds from a GST fraud by purchasing gold bullion and high-value jewellery loses the entire stock permanently to the Central Government through a confiscation order, extinguishing the claims of a bank that had a hypothecation charge on the stock, where that charge is found to have been created to defeat the Act.

A real estate developer in Hyderabad who used proceeds of a banking fraud to purchase agricultural land in Telangana faces confiscation of the land under PMLA, with all third-party sale agreements executed after attachment being declared void by the Adjudicating Authority.
what_it_covers: Any immovable or movable property determined to be proceeds of crime, upon which the Adjudicating Authority passes a final order under Section 8(6) vesting it in the Central Government.

Property on which encumbrances or lease-hold interests were created with the intent to defeat the provisions of the Act, which the Adjudicating Authority declares void and includes in the confiscation order.
Bank accounts, fixed deposits, foreign currency, gold, jewellery, vehicles, and other assets traced as proceeds of a scheduled offence and adjudicated as money-laundered property.
Property of a person charged with a scheduled offence that has been provisionally attached under Section 5 and subsequently confirmed as tainted through adjudication proceedings under Section 8.
what_it_excludes: Property that is provisionally attached under Section 5 but not yet subject to a final confiscation order under Section 8(6) — attachment is temporary and does not constitute confiscation.

Untainted property that was seized or retained along with tainted assets but is determined by the Adjudicating Authority not to be involved in money-laundering, which must be released under Section 20(5).

Property over which a legitimate encumbrance or lease-hold interest existed and was not created with the intent to defeat the Act — such genuine third-party interests survive and cannot be extinguished by a confiscation order.
Property belonging to persons not charged with or connected to a scheduled offence where no nexus to proceeds of crime is established during adjudication proceedings.
definitions.why_it_matters: A confiscation order under Section 8(6) triggers the absolute vesting of property in the Central Government under Section 9, permanently extinguishing the accused's ownership and all encumbrances, and is the ultimate penal consequence of a money-laundering adjudication. The distinction between provisional attachment and confiscation determines whether third-party rights, encumbrances, and the accused's title can still be contested or are irreversibly extinguished.

definitions.definition: "Contracting State" means any country or place outside India in respect of which arrangements have been made by the Central Government with the Government of such country through a treaty or otherwise.
definitions.plain_english: A 'contracting State' is any foreign country with which India's Central Government has made a formal arrangement — through a treaty or any other agreement — for cooperation on money laundering matters. This arrangement allows India and that foreign country to help each other in investigations, share evidence, and enforce actions related to money laundering. Only countries that have such a formal arrangement with India qualify as contracting States under this law.
real_world_examples: India enters into a Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty (MLAT) with the United States for sharing financial intelligence and evidence in money laundering cases; the USA thereby becomes a contracting State, enabling Indian authorities to send letters of request to US courts for bank records of suspects.

The Central Government signs a bilateral agreement with the United Arab Emirates (UAE) to cooperate in tracing proceeds of crime held in Dubai; UAE becomes a contracting State, allowing the Enforcement Directorate to seek freezing of assets held in UAE banks.

India and the United Kingdom have a formal arrangement enabling the Special Court in Delhi to issue a letter of request to a UK court seeking witness statements and financial documents connected to a hawala network laundering money through London.

The Central Government notifies Switzerland as a contracting State after signing a treaty for exchange of banking information; Indian investigators can formally request Swiss authorities to trace and identify properties derived from scheduled offences committed in India.

India formalises a reciprocal arrangement with Singapore under which both countries assist each other in confiscation proceedings; Singapore becomes a contracting State, allowing courts in both jurisdictions to execute each other's attachment and confiscation orders.

After signing an agreement with Mauritius, India designates it a contracting State, enabling enforcement agencies to seek evidence about shell companies used to route and launder proceeds of corruption originating in India.
what_it_covers: Any foreign country with which India has signed a Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty (MLAT) specifically covering money laundering or related offences.

Any foreign country or territory with which the Central Government has made arrangements 'otherwise' than by a formal treaty — such as executive agreements, memoranda of understanding, or diplomatic exchanges — for enforcing the provisions of the PMLA.

A country that has been notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette as one with which reciprocal arrangements have been made, subject to any specified conditions, exceptions, or qualifications.

Any jurisdiction — whether a sovereign nation or a semi-autonomous territory — outside India that has a formal bilateral arrangement with India for exchange of information and evidence in money laundering proceedings.
what_it_excludes: Countries with which India has no formal treaty or arrangement for cooperation on money laundering — even if those countries are members of international bodies like the Financial Action Task Force (FATF).
Countries that have only general diplomatic relations or trade treaties with India but no specific arrangement addressing enforcement of money laundering laws or exchange of related evidence.
Indian territories, Union Territories, or domestic jurisdictions — the definition applies exclusively to places 'outside India'.
International organisations or multilateral bodies (e.g., INTERPOL, the United Nations) that are not sovereign countries or governmental authorities of a specific country.
Countries whose arrangements with India have lapsed, been terminated, or have not been notified in the Official Gazette as required under Section 56.
definitions.why_it_matters: The designation of a country as a 'contracting State' is the gateway condition that activates the entire Chapter IX framework of the PMLA — without this status, Indian Special Courts cannot issue letters of request to foreign courts under Section 57, and India cannot render assistance to foreign courts under Section 58, meaning cross-border evidence gathering, asset tracing, and enforcement of confiscation orders remain legally impermissible. Conversely, once a country qualifies as a contracting State, Indian authorities gain enforceable channels to obtain evidence, trace proceeds of crime, and cooperate in prosecution of money laundering offences that span international boundaries.

definitions.definition: A 'contravention' refers to any act or omission that violates any of the provisions of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act or any rule, direction, or order made thereunder. It is not expressly defined in a standalone provision but is used throughout Section 70 to denote a breach of the Act's obligations, attracting penal liability upon both the company and its responsible officers.
definitions.plain_english: A contravention means breaking or going against any rule, instruction, or requirement set out in the Prevention of Money Laundering Act or any related rules or orders issued under it. If a company or its officials fail to follow what the law requires — whether by doing something prohibited or failing to do something required — that is a contravention. It can result in criminal punishment for the company and the people running it.
real_world_examples: A private limited company in Mumbai fails to maintain records of suspicious transactions as required under the PMLA, and its managing director was aware of this omission but took no corrective action — both the company and the director are liable for contravention.

A non-banking financial company (NBFC) registered in Delhi deliberately ignores a direction issued by the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU-IND) to report certain high-value cash transactions, constituting a contravention of an order made under the Act.

A real estate firm in Bengaluru, acting as a reporting entity, allows its compliance officer to suppress KYC verification records to facilitate a property deal linked to proceeds of crime — this suppression amounts to contravention of PMLA provisions.

A partnership firm providing chartered accountancy services in Chennai fails to file mandatory suspicious transaction reports (STRs) as directed under PMLA rules, and the managing partner is found to have consented to this omission — both the firm and the partner face liability for contravention.

A cooperative bank in Pune continues to process transactions for a client despite receiving an attachment order from the Adjudicating Authority, thereby contravening the order made under the Act and exposing its board members to prosecution.
what_it_covers: Any act by a company or its officers that violates a substantive provision of the PMLA, such as failure to maintain records or report suspicious transactions.
Non-compliance with a rule, direction, or order issued under the PMLA, such as ignoring an FIU directive or breaching an attachment order from the Adjudicating Authority.
Acts committed with the consent, connivance, or due to neglect of a director, manager, secretary, or other officer of the company, making such individuals personally liable.
Omissions by persons in charge of a company's business who fail to exercise due diligence to prevent a violation, even if they were not the direct perpetrators.
Violations committed by firms or associations of individuals, which are treated as companies under Section 70 for the purpose of attributing liability.
what_it_excludes: Acts that occur entirely without the knowledge of the person in charge of the company's business, provided that person exercised all due diligence to prevent the violation.

Violations of laws entirely outside the scope of the PMLA and its rules, directions, or orders — breaches of other statutes such as the Income Tax Act or Companies Act do not constitute a contravention under this section.
Civil disputes or contractual breaches between private parties that do not involve a violation of any PMLA provision, rule, direction, or order.
Actions of employees or subordinates acting entirely on their own initiative, without the knowledge, consent, connivance, or neglect of any director, manager, or officer of the company.
Procedural irregularities or technical deficiencies that do not amount to a substantive breach of any provision, rule, direction, or order under the PMLA.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as a 'contravention' under Section 70 directly determines whether both the company and its responsible officers are deemed guilty and exposed to criminal prosecution and punishment under the PMLA. It triggers the deemed liability mechanism that pierces the corporate veil, making directors and managers personally answerable unless they can establish absence of knowledge or exercise of due diligence.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of proceedings under this Act, the Special Court shall be deemed to be a Court of Session, as provided under Section 46, whereby the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 apply to proceedings before a Special Court as if it were a Court of Session. A 'Special Court' means a Court of Session designated as such under sub-section (1) of section 43.
definitions.plain_english: A Court of Session is a principal criminal court in a district in India that handles serious criminal cases. Under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, the Special Court designated to try money laundering cases is treated as a Court of Session for procedural purposes. This means all the rules of criminal procedure that apply to a Sessions Court — including bail, bonds, and trial procedures — also apply to the Special Court handling PMLA cases.
real_world_examples: An accused arrested for laundering proceeds from a hawala network in Mumbai applies for bail before the Special Court; since the Special Court is deemed a Court of Session, the bail provisions of the CrPC applicable to Sessions Courts govern the application.

A PMLA prosecution is launched in Delhi against a real estate developer alleged to have laundered money through shell companies; the Special Court designated under Section 43 conducts the trial following the same procedural rules as a District Sessions Court.

In a case involving drug money laundering in Punjab, the Public Prosecutor appointed under Section 46 presents arguments before the Special Court, and the court exercises the same powers as a Court of Session to summon witnesses and admit evidence.

An accused in a Kolkata PMLA case challenges the Special Court's jurisdiction; the court relies on Section 46 to affirm that, being deemed a Court of Session, it has full jurisdiction to try the scheduled offence along with the money-laundering charge.

In Hyderabad, a person convicted under PMLA files an appeal against the Special Court's order; since the court is deemed a Court of Session, the appeal lies to the High Court in the same manner as an appeal from a Sessions Court under the CrPC.
what_it_covers: The Special Court designated under Section 43 of PMLA when it is deemed a Court of Session for applying CrPC provisions including bail, bonds, and trial procedures.
Proceedings before the Special Court where the court exercises all powers of a Court of Session under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
The forum before which persons conducting prosecution are deemed Public Prosecutors, mirroring the position they hold before a regular Court of Session.
Any application for bail or bond made by an accused in a money laundering case, governed by CrPC provisions as if filed before a Sessions Court.
what_it_excludes: Civil courts and civil proceedings, which are governed by separate procedural law and are not deemed Courts of Session under PMLA.
The Adjudicating Authority constituted under Section 6, which handles attachment and confiscation proceedings and is not a Court of Session.
The Appellate Tribunal established under Section 25, which is an administrative tribunal and not equated to a Court of Session.
Magistrate courts below the level of Sessions Court, which are not covered by the deemed status conferred on the Special Court under Section 46.
High Courts, which are superior to Courts of Session and exercise appellate jurisdiction over the Special Court, not original PMLA trial jurisdiction.
definitions.why_it_matters: The deemed status of the Special Court as a Court of Session determines which procedural rules govern bail, evidence, and trial conduct in money laundering prosecutions, and establishes the correct appellate forum for challenging orders. If this deemed status did not apply, procedural uncertainty could arise regarding bail conditions, the appointment and qualification of prosecutors, and the manner in which the trial is conducted under the CrPC.
