definitions.definition: 'Deputy Director' means a Deputy Director appointed under sub-section (1) of section 49 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.
definitions.plain_english: A Deputy Director is a government officer formally appointed under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act to carry out enforcement functions such as investigating money laundering cases and conducting arrests. This officer works under the broader organisational hierarchy that includes the Director, Additional Director, and Joint Director. The Deputy Director holds significant statutory powers, including the power to arrest persons believed to be guilty of money laundering offences.
real_world_examples: A Deputy Director of the Enforcement Directorate (ED) in Mumbai issues a provisional attachment order against the bank accounts and real estate properties of a builder suspected of layering proceeds from an illegal hawala network through shell companies.

A Deputy Director posted at the ED's Delhi Zonal Office conducts a search and seizure operation at the offices of a cryptocurrency exchange suspected of laundering funds linked to online fraud, recording reasons in writing before exercising powers under the Act.

During a money laundering investigation linked to a chit fund scam in Kolkata, a Deputy Director authorised by the Director arrests the promoter of the fraudulent scheme under Section 19 of the Act after gathering sufficient material evidence.

A Deputy Director in Chennai, authorised by the Director under Section 5, provisionally attaches agricultural land and gold ornaments valued at several crores, which are alleged to be proceeds of crime from a drug trafficking scheduled offence.

A Deputy Director stationed at the ED's Hyderabad office issues summons to the directors of a non-banking financial company under investigation for siphoning depositor funds through fictitious loan disbursements and routing the proceeds abroad.
what_it_covers: An officer formally appointed by the Central Government under sub-section (1) of Section 49 of PMLA with the specific designation of 'Deputy Director'.
An officer empowered to provisionally attach property under Section 5 when authorised by the Director, upon recording reasons to believe that proceeds of crime are involved.
An officer vested with the power to arrest a person under Section 19 where there is reason to believe, based on material in possession, that the person is guilty of an offence under the Act.
An officer who may be authorised by the Director to exercise specific investigative and enforcement functions under the Act, forming part of the PMLA enforcement hierarchy.
what_it_excludes: Officers holding the rank of Director, Additional Director, or Joint Director, who are separately defined under Section 2 read with Section 49 of the Act.
An Assistant Director appointed under Section 49(1), who is a distinct lower-ranking officer with a separate definition under the Act.
Police officers, CBI officials, or any other investigating officers not appointed specifically under sub-section (1) of Section 49 of PMLA, even if they hold an equivalent rank in their own cadre.
State government officers or revenue intelligence officers who may investigate predicate offences but are not appointed as Deputy Directors under PMLA.
Any officer exercising powers merely by administrative delegation outside the formal appointment process prescribed under Section 49(1) of the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of an officer as a 'Deputy Director' is critical because only such a designated officer (or one authorised by the Director) can lawfully exercise coercive powers under PMLA — including provisional attachment of property under Section 5 and arrest under Section 19 — making the formal appointment a jurisdictional prerequisite for valid enforcement action. Any action taken by a person not holding this designation or not duly authorised under the Act would be without jurisdiction and liable to be set aside.

definitions.definition: An encumbrance, as used in Section 9 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, refers to any charge, lien, mortgage, claim, liability, lease-hold interest, or other right or interest created over a property that diminishes its value or restricts its free transfer, which upon confiscation must be extinguished so that the property vests absolutely in the Central Government free from all such burdens. Where the Adjudicating Authority finds that an encumbrance has been created with a view to defeat the provisions of Chapter III, it may declare such encumbrance void.
definitions.plain_english: An encumbrance is any kind of legal claim, burden, or charge that someone else has over a property — such as a bank loan secured against it, a mortgage, or a lease given to a tenant. When the government confiscates a property under money laundering law, all such claims are wiped out and the government gets the property completely free and clear. However, if someone deliberately created a fake loan or lease on a property just to prevent the government from taking it, the court can declare that arrangement invalid.
real_world_examples: A person accused of money laundering mortgages his Mumbai flat to a cooperative bank before confiscation proceedings begin. Upon the confiscation order under Section 8(6), the property vests in the Central Government free from this mortgage encumbrance, though the bank may pursue a civil suit for damages against the accused.

A hawala operator creates a lease agreement in favour of his relative for a commercial property in Delhi for a 30-year term, just to complicate government confiscation. The Adjudicating Authority, after hearing the relative, declares the lease-hold interest void as it was created to defeat the provisions of Chapter III, and the property vests free from that encumbrance.

A real estate developer accused of laundering funds through shell companies had taken a construction finance loan from an NBFC, secured by a charge on the land parcel. After confiscation, the Central Government acquires the land free from the NBFC's charge, but the NBFC retains the right to file a suit for damages against the accused developer.

A Bengaluru businessman under PMLA investigation registers a usufructuary mortgage on his commercial plot in favour of a family trust to reduce its apparent free-hold value and deter attachment. The Adjudicating Authority, finding the mortgage was fraudulently created, declares it void under the proviso to Section 9, allowing the Central Government to take the property unencumbered.

A person involved in a Ponzi scheme in Kolkata had granted an agricultural lease on attached rural land to a tenant company controlled by associates. On confiscation, the Adjudicating Authority examines whether the lease was genuine or a device to defeat confiscation, and if found fraudulent, declares it void so the land vests absolutely in the Central Government.
what_it_covers: Mortgages registered over a property by the accused to secure loans from banks or financial institutions prior to or during confiscation proceedings.
Lease-hold interests or long-term lease agreements granted in favour of relatives, associates, or shell entities with the intent to defeat confiscation under Chapter III.
Liens, charges, hypothecations, or other security interests created over the attached or confiscated property in favour of creditors or third parties.
Usufructuary mortgages, equitable mortgages, or any other form of security interest that diminishes the free-hold title of the property.
Any right or interest in the property created with a view to reduce its net value or complicate the government's ability to vest it absolutely.
what_it_excludes: Personal liabilities of the accused that are not secured against the specific confiscated property — these survive confiscation and can be enforced by suit for damages against the accused personally.

Genuine, bona fide encumbrances created in good faith before any money laundering activity began, where the creditor had no knowledge of the proceeds of crime — such creditors retain the right to seek damages by civil suit.

Statutory charges or government dues such as unpaid property taxes or utility arrears that operate by operation of law rather than by private agreement, which are treated separately under applicable municipal or revenue laws.

Rights arising under a valid court decree or order made prior to the attachment, which are assessed independently and are not extinguished merely by the confiscation order without specific adjudication.

Tenancy rights protected under state rent control legislation where the tenancy predates and is entirely unconnected with the money laundering offence, as these may not be treated as encumbrances created to defeat confiscation.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence or absence of an encumbrance directly determines whether the Central Government receives clean, unencumbered title to confiscated property upon a confiscation order under Section 8(6), or whether third-party claims survive and complicate the State's recovery. If the Adjudicating Authority finds an encumbrance was created to defeat confiscation, it declares it void, preventing accused persons from using fraudulent charges or leases as a shield to retain effective control over proceeds of crime.

definitions.definition: 'financial institution' means a financial institution as defined in clause (c) of section 45-I of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (2 of 1934) and includes a chit fund company, a co-operative bank, a housing finance institution and a non-banking financial company.
definitions.plain_english: A financial institution is any organisation that provides financial services such as lending, investment, or managing funds, as recognised under the Reserve Bank of India Act. This includes chit fund companies, cooperative banks, housing finance companies, and non-banking financial companies (NBFCs). These entities are not full commercial banks but still handle significant sums of money and are therefore subject to anti-money laundering rules.
real_world_examples: A housing finance company like LIC Housing Finance providing home loans is a financial institution and must maintain transaction records and report suspicious activity to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-IND) under the PMLA.

An NBFC like Bajaj Finance Ltd, which offers consumer loans and investment products, is classified as a financial institution and is obligated to conduct KYC verification and report cash transactions above prescribed thresholds.

A state-level cooperative bank in Maharashtra accepting deposits and issuing loans to its members falls within the definition and must comply with PMLA obligations including maintaining records under Section 12.

A chit fund company registered in Tamil Nadu conducting monthly chit auctions is treated as a financial institution under PMLA, making it liable for reporting obligations and susceptible to investigation if proceeds of crime flow through its operations.

An NBFC-MFI (Microfinance Institution) disbursing small loans to rural borrowers in Uttar Pradesh qualifies as a financial institution and must file Suspicious Transaction Reports if any borrower's transactions indicate layering of illicit funds.
what_it_covers: Financial institutions as defined under clause (c) of section 45-I of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, including entities engaged in the business of providing finance.
Chit fund companies that manage, conduct or supervise chits as defined under the Chit Funds Act, 1982.
Co-operative banks as defined under the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation Act, 1961.
Housing finance institutions as defined under clause (d) of section 2 of the National Housing Bank Act, 1987.
Non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) as defined under clause (f) of section 45-I of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.
what_it_excludes: Banking companies, which are separately defined under the PMLA as companies or co-operative banks to which the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 applies, and are treated as a distinct category.
Intermediaries such as stock-brokers, portfolio managers, and investment advisers registered under SEBI, which are governed under a separate definition in the Act.
Insurance companies and entities regulated solely under the Insurance Act, 1938, which are not expressly included in the financial institution definition under PMLA.
Individuals or unregistered moneylenders operating outside the formal regulatory framework of the RBI Act, who do not qualify as financial institutions under this definition.
Pure trading or manufacturing companies that may advance inter-corporate loans but are not engaged in the business of finance as envisaged under the RBI Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Entities that qualify as 'financial institutions' under PMLA are subject to mandatory obligations under Sections 11, 12, 13, 14, and 15, including maintaining records of transactions, verifying client identity, and reporting suspicious transactions to authorities; failure to comply constitutes a contravention attracting penalties and prosecution. The definition also determines whether the Adjudicating Authority can compel the attendance and document production of officers of such entities and whether the Director can exercise investigative powers against them.

definitions.definition: Financial institutions, as used in the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, refer to entities other than banking companies that are engaged in financial activities, including housing finance institutions, chit fund companies, co-operative banks, non-banking financial companies, and any other institution carrying on the business of financial intermediation as notified by the Central Government. Such institutions are obligated to maintain records of transactions, verify client identities, and furnish information to the Director in the prescribed manner.
definitions.plain_english: A financial institution is any organisation that deals with money and financial services but is not a traditional bank. This includes companies like housing loan providers, non-banking finance companies (NBFCs), chit funds, and co-operative banks. These organisations are required under anti-money laundering law to keep detailed records of their transactions and report suspicious activity to government authorities.
real_world_examples: HDFC Ltd. (before its merger), operating as a housing finance company in India, was required under PMLA to maintain records of all large loan disbursements and report suspicious transactions to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-IND).

A chit fund company operating in Tamil Nadu must verify the identity of all its subscribers and maintain transaction records for at least ten years, as it qualifies as a financial institution under PMLA.

Mahindra Finance, a registered NBFC, is obligated to report any customer who makes unusually large repayments in cash or structurally broken payments below the prescribed threshold to evade detection, to the Director under PMLA.

A co-operative bank in Maharashtra providing agricultural loans must comply with KYC norms and furnish records of suspicious transactions to the FIU-IND, since it qualifies as a financial institution under the Act.

Bajaj Finance Ltd., an NBFC offering consumer loans, is subject to PMLA obligations and must flag and report transactions where the source of funds appears to be proceeds of crime, failing which its principal officer may be penalised.
what_it_covers: Housing finance institutions such as LIC Housing Finance or PNB Housing Finance that provide mortgage and home loans.
Non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) registered with the Reserve Bank of India that engage in lending, investment, or asset financing activities.
Chit fund companies registered under the Chit Funds Act, 1982, that pool and distribute funds among subscribers.
Co-operative banks operating at state or district level that accept deposits and provide credit facilities.
Any other institution notified by the Central Government as a financial institution for the purposes of PMLA compliance.
what_it_excludes: Banking companies as defined under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, which are separately categorised and governed under PMLA.
Intermediaries such as stockbrokers, mutual fund agents, and insurance intermediaries, which form a distinct category under PMLA.
Individuals acting as moneylenders under state moneylending acts who are not incorporated entities engaged in systematic financial intermediation.
Government departments or ministries that disburse funds but do not engage in commercial financial intermediation.
Pure payment aggregators or technology companies that facilitate transactions without holding or lending funds, unless separately notified.

This classification also determines the scope of rule-making power under Section 73, as the Central Government may prescribe specific compliance procedures applicable to financial institutions.

definitions.definition: The term 'fine' is not separately defined in Section 2 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. As used in the Act, 'fine' denotes a monetary penalty imposed by a competent authority — including the Special Court under Section 4 and the Director under Section 13 — as a punitive or regulatory sanction upon a person or entity found guilty of or in contravention of the provisions of the Act, including the offence of money-laundering or failure to comply with reporting obligations. Under Section 4, fine may extend to five lakh rupees, and under Section 69, fine is referenced in the context of recovery of sums due to the Central Government.
definitions.plain_english: A 'fine' under this law is a sum of money that a court or authorized authority orders someone to pay as a punishment for breaking the rules of the law. For example, if someone is convicted of money laundering, they can be ordered to pay a fine of up to five lakh rupees in addition to going to prison. Similarly, banks or financial institutions that fail to maintain proper records or report suspicious transactions can be fined by the Director. The fine must be paid to the government.
real_world_examples: A person convicted by the Special Court in Mumbai for laundering proceeds from a drug trafficking operation is sentenced to five years of rigorous imprisonment and ordered to pay a fine of five lakh rupees under Section 4 of the PMLA.

A private bank in Delhi fails to file Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) as required under Section 12; the Director, after inquiry under Section 13, imposes a monetary fine on the bank and its principal officer for non-compliance.

An intermediary registered with SEBI in Hyderabad does not maintain records of client transactions as mandated under the PMLA; upon detection during an investigation, the Director levies a fine recoverable as arrears of land revenue under Section 69.

A hawala operator in Chennai is prosecuted before the Special Court for money-laundering linked to a scheduled offence under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act; upon conviction, the court imposes the maximum fine of five lakh rupees alongside rigorous imprisonment.

A cooperative bank in Pune is found to have repeatedly failed to report cash transactions above the prescribed threshold; the Director imposes a fine which, upon non-payment, is recovered by the Central Government using the recovery mechanism under Section 69.
what_it_covers: Fine imposed by the Special Court upon conviction of the offence of money-laundering under Section 4, up to five lakh rupees (or applicable limit for scheduled offences under paragraph 2 of Part A).

Monetary penalty imposed by the Director under Section 13 on banking companies, financial institutions, or intermediaries that fail to comply with record-keeping and reporting obligations under Section 12.
Sums recoverable as fine by the Central Government under Section 69 as arrears of land revenue when a person defaults on payment of any amount due under the Act.
Fine imposed in relation to any scheduled offence that is predicate to money-laundering, where the quantum of fine is determined by the relevant provisions of the Act.
what_it_excludes: Attachment and confiscation of property, which are distinct civil remedies under Chapter III of the PMLA and do not constitute a 'fine' even though they result in financial loss to the accused.
Rigorous imprisonment, which is a separate and independent component of the punishment under Section 4 and is not subsumed within the concept of fine.
Compensation or restitution ordered in favour of a victim or third party, which is not a fine payable to the government but rather a civil remedy.

Penalty or interest levied under other fiscal statutes such as the Income Tax Act or Customs Act, even if connected to the same underlying transaction, as those are governed by their respective enactments and not by the PMLA.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a fine is imposed, and its quantum, directly determines the punitive financial consequence for a person convicted of money-laundering under Section 4 or an entity in contravention of Section 12; non-payment of a fine triggers the recovery mechanism under Section 69, enabling the Central Government to recover the amount as arrears of land revenue, thereby creating an enforceable debt obligation against the defaulter's assets.

definitions.definition: The term 'good faith' is not formally defined in the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, but as used in Section 67, it refers to any act done or intended to be done honestly, without fraud, deceit, or malicious intent, by the Government or any officer of the Government in the discharge of their duties under the Act, even if such act is done with some degree of error or negligence, provided there is no deliberate wrongdoing.
definitions.plain_english: Good faith means acting honestly and sincerely, without any intention to deceive or harm anyone. If a government officer does something under this law genuinely believing it is the right and lawful thing to do — even if they make a mistake — they are said to have acted in good faith. This protects officers from being sued or prosecuted for honest mistakes made while doing their official duties under the law.
real_world_examples: An Enforcement Directorate officer in Mumbai attaches a property belonging to a suspect based on available intelligence reports, which later turns out to be owned by an unrelated third party — since the officer acted on genuine belief and available evidence without malice, the act is covered under good faith.

A Director at the Financial Intelligence Unit issues summons to a banking company in Delhi for records related to a suspected money laundering transaction, but inadvertently cites an incorrect provision of the Act — since the intent was honest enforcement of the law, the action qualifies as done in good faith.

During a search operation in Bengaluru, an investigating officer seizes documents from a company's office believing them to be proceeds of crime records, but the documents are later found to be irrelevant — the officer's action, being based on reasonable belief and not malice, is protected under the good faith clause.

A Joint Director in Chennai orders freezing of a bank account of an individual suspected of money laundering based on preliminary information that later proves insufficient — because the order was made with honest intent and no personal motive, the officer cannot be sued in a civil court for such action.

A government officer conducting a survey under the Act in Hyderabad inadvertently causes minor disruption to a legitimate business operation while investigating an inter-connected transaction — since no bad faith or corrupt motive is involved, both the officer and the Government are shielded from civil liability.
what_it_covers: Actions taken by Enforcement Directorate officers in attaching, seizing, or freezing property based on genuine belief of money laundering, even if the belief later proves incorrect.
Orders issued by the Director or Deputy Director under the Act that are based on honest assessment of available information, even if procedurally imperfect.
Any prosecution, suit, or other proceeding initiated by a government officer under the Act with sincere intent to enforce the law, without any malicious or fraudulent motive.
Acts intended to be done under the Act, meaning even preparatory or incomplete actions taken with honest intent are protected before they are fully executed.
The Government of India as an entity when its officers act in discharge of their duties under the Act without dishonesty or corrupt intent.
what_it_excludes: Actions taken by a government officer with deliberate malice, personal vendetta, or corrupt intent against a specific individual, even if done under the guise of enforcing the Act.
Acts that are fraudulent or involve intentional misrepresentation by an officer, such as fabricating evidence or knowingly filing false records to implicate an innocent person.
Actions of private parties or non-government persons, as the good faith protection under Section 67 expressly applies only to the Government and officers of the Government.
Proceedings that are wholly unrelated to the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, even if conducted by government officers in some official capacity.
Cases where gross negligence or reckless disregard for a person's rights is demonstrated, which may be distinguished from honest mistake or bona fide error in legal interpretation.
definitions.why_it_matters: The application of 'good faith' under Section 67 is decisive in determining whether a civil suit can be maintained against the Government or its officers for actions taken under the Act — if an officer acted in good faith, no such suit or prosecution can proceed, providing complete immunity. Conversely, if bad faith or malicious intent is established, the bar under Section 67 does not apply, and the officer or Government may face civil or criminal liability.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 42, 'High Court' means the High Court within the jurisdiction of which the aggrieved party ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain; and where the Central Government is the aggrieved party, the High Court within the jurisdiction of which the respondent, or in a case where there are more than one respondent, any of the respondents, ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain. For the purposes of Section 43, 'High Court' means the High Court of the State in which a Sessions Court designated as Special Court was functioning immediately before such designation.
definitions.plain_english: The 'High Court' under this law refers to the specific High Court that has authority over a case based on where the affected person lives, works, or does business. If the government is the party challenging a decision, then the relevant High Court is the one covering the area where the other party lives or works. For setting up Special Courts to try money laundering offences, the High Court meant is the one in the State where that Sessions Court is located.
real_world_examples: A businessman from Mumbai who is aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Tribunal would file his appeal before the Bombay High Court, since that is within whose jurisdiction he ordinarily carries on business.
Where the Central Government challenges a ruling of the Appellate Tribunal and the respondent is a company registered and operating in Chennai, the appeal would be filed before the Madras High Court.

When the Central Government issues a notification to designate a Sessions Court in Kolkata as a Special Court under Section 43 for money laundering trials, it does so in consultation with the Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court, which is the High Court of that State.

An individual accused of money laundering who ordinarily resides in Pune appeals against an Appellate Tribunal order; the Bombay High Court, within whose jurisdiction Pune falls, would be the appropriate High Court to hear the appeal under Section 42.

A non-banking financial company headquartered in Hyderabad contests an Appellate Tribunal decision; the appeal lies before the Telangana High Court as it is the court within whose jurisdiction the company carries on business.

If a Central Government appeal concerns multiple respondents residing in different States, such as Delhi and Bengaluru, the Central Government may choose to file the appeal before either the Delhi High Court or the Karnataka High Court, as any one respondent's location suffices.
semantic_tags: State High Court Special Court designation
what_it_covers: The High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the aggrieved private party ordinarily resides, carries on business, or personally works for gain, for the purpose of appeals under Section 42.
The High Court within whose jurisdiction any one of the respondents resides or carries on business, where the Central Government is the appellant under Section 42.
The High Court of the State in which a Sessions Court was functioning before being designated as a Special Court under Section 43, for the purpose of consultation on that designation.
High Courts of all States and Union Territories with a High Court, to the extent that the aggrieved party or respondent falls within their respective territorial jurisdictions under this Act.
what_it_excludes: The Supreme Court of India, which is a separate constitutional court and not included within the meaning of 'High Court' as defined for these sections.
District Courts, Sessions Courts, Magistrate Courts, and other subordinate courts, which do not constitute a 'High Court' for the purposes of Sections 42 and 43.
A High Court of a State where neither the aggrieved party nor any respondent resides, works, or carries on business, as it would lack the jurisdictional nexus required under Section 42.
The Appellate Tribunal itself, which is a separate quasi-judicial body and not a High Court for the purposes of this Act.
High Courts of foreign jurisdictions or international appellate bodies, which are entirely outside the scope of this definition.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'High Court' directly determines which court has jurisdiction to hear appeals against Appellate Tribunal orders under Section 42, and filing before the wrong court could render the appeal invalid or time-barred. Under Section 43, it determines which Chief Justice must be consulted before Special Courts for money laundering trials are designated, making the consultation a mandatory prerequisite to valid court designation.

definitions.definition: 'housing finance institution' shall have the meaning as assigned to it in clause (d) of section 2 of the National Housing Bank Act, 1987 (53 of 1987).
definitions.plain_english: A housing finance institution is a company that is primarily in the business of providing loans and financial assistance for buying, building, or repairing homes and residential properties. These institutions are specifically recognized under the National Housing Bank Act, 1987 and are supervised by the National Housing Bank. Examples include companies like HDFC Ltd., LIC Housing Finance, and similar home loan providers in India.
real_world_examples: HDFC Ltd. (now merged with HDFC Bank) disbursing home loans to individuals purchasing residential flats in Mumbai — it qualifies as a housing finance institution and is thus subject to PMLA obligations.

LIC Housing Finance Limited providing construction finance to a real estate developer in Bengaluru for a residential township project — as a housing finance institution, it must maintain records and report suspicious transactions under PMLA.

A regional housing finance company registered with National Housing Bank offering loans for house repairs and renovations in rural Rajasthan — it falls under this definition and must comply with Know Your Customer (KYC) and Anti-Money Laundering norms.

PNB Housing Finance Limited sanctioning a large mortgage loan to a borrower whose funds are later found to be proceeds of crime — the institution's classification as a housing finance institution triggers its reporting duties and liability under PMLA.

Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited flagging an unusually large prepayment of a home loan by a customer with no apparent legitimate income source — as a housing finance institution under PMLA, it is obligated to file a Suspicious Transaction Report with the Financial Intelligence Unit-India.
what_it_covers: Companies primarily engaged in providing long-term finance for construction or purchase of residential houses, as recognized under clause (d) of section 2 of the National Housing Bank Act, 1987.
Housing finance companies registered with and regulated by the National Housing Bank, such as HDFC Ltd., LIC Housing Finance, and PNB Housing Finance.
Institutions providing finance for renovation, repair, or reconstruction of existing residential properties, falling within the ambit of the National Housing Bank Act definition.
Housing finance institutions that also extend finance to builders and developers for construction of residential properties intended for individual purchase.
what_it_excludes: Scheduled commercial banks (such as SBI or ICICI Bank) that offer home loan products — these are classified separately as 'banking companies' under PMLA, not housing finance institutions.
Non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) that do not primarily engage in housing finance and are not registered as housing finance institutions with the National Housing Bank.
Pure real estate developers or construction companies that build and sell residential properties but do not provide financial loans or credit for housing purposes.

Co-operative banks and co-operative credit societies that may incidentally finance housing but are not specifically classified as housing finance institutions under the National Housing Bank Act, 1987.
General insurance or life insurance companies that invest in mortgage-backed securities but do not directly provide housing finance to end consumers.
definitions.why_it_matters: Classifying an entity as a 'housing finance institution' brings it within the definition of 'financial institution' under PMLA, making it a reporting entity subject to obligations such as maintaining transaction records, filing Suspicious Transaction Reports, and conducting customer due diligence — failure to comply can attract prosecution and penalties under the Act. It also means that any property or funds laundered through such an institution can be attached and confiscated, and the institution's officers may face liability for knowingly facilitating money laundering.

definitions.definition: "Identifying" includes establishment of a proof that the property was derived from, or used in the commission of an offence under section 3.
definitions.plain_english: Identifying means proving that a particular piece of property is connected to money laundering — either because it came from criminal activity or was used to carry out the crime. It is the process of establishing a clear link between the property and the illegal offence. This is a key step authorities take when tracing assets suspected to be proceeds of crime.
real_world_examples: The Enforcement Directorate traces bank accounts linked to a hawala network and establishes documentary proof that funds deposited in those accounts originated from drug trafficking proceeds, thereby identifying the property under PMLA.

In a corruption case involving a Maharashtra government official, investigators gather bank statements, property registration records, and witness statements to prove that a luxury apartment was purchased using bribe money, identifying it as property derived from the scheduled offence.

Following a letter of request from a contracting State such as the UAE, Indian authorities examine financial records of an NRI businessman to establish that real estate holdings in Mumbai were funded through proceeds of a fraud committed abroad, thus identifying the property.

During a GST fraud investigation, the Director forwards a letter of request under Section 59 and authorities conduct a survey of company premises to prove that certain machinery and inventory were acquired using funds generated through tax evasion, identifying them as property used in or derived from the offence under section 3.

In a cyber fraud case, the Enforcement Directorate analyses digital transaction trails and cryptocurrency wallet records to establish proof that Bitcoin holdings in an accused's wallet were directly derived from phishing scam proceeds, identifying the virtual assets as proceeds of crime.
what_it_covers: Establishing documentary proof — such as bank records, title deeds, and transaction logs — that property was directly derived from proceeds of the offence of money laundering under section 3.
Proving that a specific property, movable or immovable, was used as an instrument in committing the offence under section 3, even if it was not itself generated by the crime.

Identification activities carried out pursuant to a letter of request from a contracting State, where Indian authorities must prove the link between property located in India and a foreign predicate offence.
Inquiries, investigations, or surveys conducted by authorised authorities to gather sufficient evidence to establish the required proof of connection between property and the scheduled offence.
what_it_excludes: Mere suspicion or intelligence input about a property's criminal origin, without establishment of proof, does not constitute 'identifying' under this definition.

Tracing the movement, source, or ownership of property without establishing proof of its connection to the offence under section 3 — that process falls under 'tracing' as separately defined in this Chapter.
Identification of persons or individuals involved in money laundering, as the definition is specifically limited to establishing proof in relation to property, not to identifying accused persons.
Property linked to offences other than those constituting the offence under section 3 of PMLA, since the definition explicitly requires proof of derivation from or use in that specific offence.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a property has been successfully 'identified' determines whether authorities can proceed with its attachment, seizure, and confiscation under Chapter III of PMLA; without establishing this proof, no valid order of attachment or confiscation can be sustained. It is also the prerequisite condition that must be fulfilled when executing letters of request from contracting States under Section 60, making it a gateway obligation for international asset recovery cooperation.

definitions.definition: "Information" under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act refers to any data, particulars, records, or details pertaining to transactions, identity of clients, sources of income, earnings or assets, or any other material that banking companies, financial institutions, intermediaries, or persons are required to furnish to the Director or any authority under the Act. It includes information disclosed pursuant to notices issued by the Adjudicating Authority as well as transaction records mandatorily reported under Section 12, and extends to any intelligence shared between authorities under Section 66 for the purposes of investigating or preventing money laundering.
definitions.plain_english: "Information" means any facts, data, documents, or details that a bank, financial institution, intermediary, or any person must share with the government authorities under this law. This could be details about financial transactions, the identity of customers, or the source of someone's wealth. It is the raw material that government investigators use to detect and prosecute money laundering. Sharing this information correctly is a legal obligation, and withholding it can lead to penalties.
real_world_examples: A nationalised bank in Mumbai detects a series of cash deposits just below the prescribed threshold (structuring) in a customer's account and furnishes a Suspicious Transaction Report containing transaction details, customer KYC data, and account history to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-IND) under the Director — this constitutes 'information' under the Act.

The Enforcement Directorate issues a notice to a Hyderabad-based real estate developer under Section 8, directing him to submit details of the sources of income, asset ownership records, sale deeds, and bank statements used to acquire properties that have been provisionally attached — all such particulars submitted constitute 'information'.

definitions.definition: Inter-connected transactions refer to two or more transactions that are linked to each other as part of a money-laundering scheme, such that where one or more of such transactions is proved to be involved in money-laundering, the remaining transactions shall be presumed, unless otherwise proved to the satisfaction of the Adjudicating Authority, to also form part of the money-laundering activity for purposes of adjudication or confiscation under section 8.
definitions.plain_english: Inter-connected transactions are two or more financial dealings that are linked together as part of a money-laundering scheme. If authorities can prove that even one of these linked transactions involves money laundering, the law automatically assumes the remaining connected transactions are also part of the same illegal activity. The person accused must then prove to the Adjudicating Authority that the other transactions are innocent and unrelated.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based real estate developer receives Rs. 5 crore in cash from an unknown source, immediately transfers Rs. 3 crore to a shell company in Delhi, which then purchases a commercial plot in Pune — all three transactions are inter-connected and if the initial cash receipt is proved to be proceeds of crime, the subsequent transfers and property purchase are presumed to be part of the same money-laundering scheme.

A hawala operator in Hyderabad collects Rs. 2 crore from a drug trafficker, converts it into gold jewellery through one transaction, sells the jewellery through a trader and deposits the proceeds in a bank account through another transaction — if the initial hawala transfer is proved to involve money laundering, the gold purchase and bank deposit are presumed to be inter-connected money-laundering transactions.

A Kolkata-based businessman receives illicit funds from a Ponzi scheme operator, uses one transaction to buy foreign currency, and a second transaction to wire the funds to a Dubai account — if ED proves the foreign currency purchase is linked to proceeds of crime, the international wire transfer is presumed to be part of the inter-connected money-laundering chain.

In a Delhi corruption case, a government official's wife first deposits bribe money in a cooperative bank (transaction one), then invests it in a chit fund company (transaction two), and finally purchases residential property in Gurugram (transaction three) — proving transaction one involves money laundering creates a legal presumption that transactions two and three are also inter-connected money-laundering transactions.

A Chennai-based company receives fraudulent loan proceeds from a bank, rotates the funds through three separate subsidiary company accounts in quick succession, and finally invests in stock market shares — if the initial fraudulent receipt is proved, all intermediate transfers and the final investment are presumed to be inter-connected transactions forming part of the money-laundering operation.
what_it_covers: A series of financial transactions structured in sequence where funds move from one account or asset to another as part of a deliberate money-laundering scheme.
Transactions across different entities, persons, or geographies that are factually or documentarily linked to a common source of proceeds of crime.
Transactions that occur within a short time frame or follow a discernible pattern suggesting they were designed together to disguise the origin of illicit funds.
Transactions involving different instruments such as cash deposits, property purchases, share investments, or foreign remittances that collectively serve to launder a single pool of tainted money.
Cases where intermediate transactions are conducted through nominees, shell companies, or third parties but are traceable back to the original proceeds of crime.
what_it_excludes: Transactions that are entirely independent of each other with no factual, documentary, or temporal link to a proved money-laundering transaction.

Routine commercial or personal financial transactions that coincidentally occur around the same time as a money-laundering transaction but have a legitimate, independent explanation satisfying the Adjudicating Authority.
Transactions involving untainted property or funds that are demonstrably sourced from legitimate income and are proved to be unconnected to the proceeds of crime.
Transactions completed before the underlying scheduled offence was committed, as they cannot logically be connected to proceeds arising from a future offence.
Transactions between parties who have no knowledge of or connection to the money-laundering scheme and can establish bona fide dealings to the satisfaction of the Adjudicating Authority.
definitions.why_it_matters: The concept of inter-connected transactions activates a critical statutory presumption under Section 23 that reverses the burden of proof — once one transaction in a chain is proved to involve money laundering, all remaining connected transactions are presumed tainted, enabling the Adjudicating Authority to order attachment and confiscation of all associated properties under Section 8 unless the accused disproves the connection. This provision dramatically expands the scope of confiscation and adjudication, making it legally sufficient to prove just one link in a complex multi-layered laundering scheme.

definitions.definition: As used in the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, 'intermediaries' refers to entities such as stock brokers, sub-brokers, share transfer agents, bankers to an issue, trustees of a trust deed, registrars to an issue, merchant bankers, underwriters, portfolio managers, investment advisers, and any other intermediary associated with securities markets and registered under section 12 of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, as well as other entities prescribed by the Central Government, who are obligated to maintain records of transactions, furnish information to the Director, and verify client identities under Section 12 of this Act.
definitions.plain_english: Intermediaries are businesses or professionals that sit between clients and financial markets or services — such as stockbrokers, mutual fund distributors, portfolio managers, and similar market participants registered with regulators like SEBI. Under the anti-money laundering law, they must keep detailed records of client transactions, report suspicious or large transactions to the government's Financial Intelligence Unit, and verify who their clients are. They play a critical role as gatekeepers to prevent the financial system from being misused for money laundering.
real_world_examples: A SEBI-registered stockbroker in Mumbai notices a client making multiple large cash-equivalent transactions in penny stocks within a single month; the broker is required as an 'intermediary' to report these to the Director (FIU-IND) and maintain records for ten years.

A portfolio management services (PMS) provider registered with SEBI onboards a high-net-worth individual and must conduct KYC verification and maintain identity records as mandated under Section 12, in its capacity as an intermediary under PMLA.

A registrar and transfer agent (RTA) handling share transfers for a listed company is classified as an intermediary and must flag and report transactions that appear to be structured below the prescribed value to evade reporting thresholds.

A merchant banker managing an IPO is treated as an intermediary under PMLA and must verify the identity of all investors applying through it, maintain those records, and furnish information to FIU-IND when suspicious transaction patterns are detected.

An investment adviser registered under SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, advising clients on securities portfolios, must comply with PMLA record-keeping and reporting obligations in its role as an intermediary, including flagging unusual investment patterns that may indicate layering of illicit funds.
what_it_covers: SEBI-registered stockbrokers and sub-brokers who execute securities transactions on behalf of clients and are required to maintain transaction records and report to FIU-IND.
Portfolio managers, investment advisers, and mutual fund distributors registered under SEBI regulations who manage or advise on client investments in securities markets.
Registrars to an issue, share transfer agents, merchant bankers, underwriters, and trustees of trust deeds who are involved in capital market operations and registered under SEBI Act, section 12.
Any other entity notified by the Central Government or prescribed under rules as an intermediary for the purposes of PMLA compliance obligations.
Bankers to a public issue who handle application money and are associated with securities market transactions, thereby falling under intermediary obligations.
what_it_excludes: Banking companies, which are separately and distinctly categorized under PMLA and governed by their own regulatory framework under the Reserve Bank of India Act, even though they share similar record-keeping obligations.

Financial institutions as defined separately under PMLA (such as housing finance institutions, non-banking financial companies at the statutory level), which are treated as a distinct category from intermediaries in Sections 12 and 14.

Ordinary individuals or unregistered agents who facilitate transactions informally without being registered with a regulatory body such as SEBI, and thus do not fall within the statutory definition of intermediaries.
Government departments or public sector undertakings that may conduct financial transactions but are not registered as market intermediaries with SEBI or any other prescribed regulator.

Legal professionals such as advocates or chartered accountants acting in their professional advisory capacity who are not registered as intermediaries under any securities or financial market regulation.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as an 'intermediary' under PMLA directly determines whether it is legally bound to maintain transaction records, verify client identities, and report to FIU-IND under Section 12 — failure to comply constitutes an offence attracting penalties under Section 13. Conversely, an intermediary that furnishes such information in good faith is granted immunity from civil proceedings under Section 14, making the classification critical for both compliance obligations and legal protection.

definitions.definition: An 'investigating officer' under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act means an officer authorised to conduct investigation into an offence of money laundering under this Act, including conducting searches and seizures under sections 17 and 18, retaining seized records under section 21, and making applications to a Special Court for letters of request to contracting States under section 57. The term encompasses officers of the Directorate of Enforcement empowered to investigate money laundering offences and exercise powers incidental thereto.
definitions.plain_english: An investigating officer is a government official, typically from the Enforcement Directorate, who is officially assigned to look into cases of money laundering under this law. They have the power to search premises, seize documents and records, and gather evidence both within India and from foreign countries. Think of them as the law enforcement officer responsible for building the case against someone suspected of laundering money.

definitions.plain_english: An 'investigation' under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act refers to any formal proceeding carried out by the Enforcement Directorate's Director or another government-authorised authority to gather evidence about possible money laundering. This includes activities like searching premises, recording statements, seizing documents, and examining witnesses. The word 'includes' makes this an open-ended definition, meaning it covers a wide range of evidence-collection activities and is not limited to a narrow set of actions.
real_world_examples: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) initiates proceedings against a Bollywood producer suspected of layering film financing through shell companies in Mumbai — all search operations, statement recordings, and document seizures conducted during this process constitute 'investigation' under PMLA.

A Deputy Director of the ED examines on oath the CFO of a Gurugram-based fintech startup suspected of routing hawala money through merchant accounts; the entire examination and evidence-collection exercise is an 'investigation' under this Act.

The Central Government authorises a special task force to collect evidence against a Kolkata-based jeweller accused of converting proceeds from illegal mining into gold purchases; all proceedings conducted by that task force amount to an 'investigation' under PMLA.

After a predicate scheduled offence (such as drug trafficking) is registered against a Delhi-based real estate developer, the ED Director orders search and seizure of property records and bank statements — these proceedings for evidence collection qualify as 'investigation' under the Act.

During a cross-border money laundering probe linked to a Punjab-based non-banking financial company, the Director issues summons to company directors and records their statements — this evidence-gathering process is treated as an 'investigation' under PMLA, giving the proceedings formal legal authority.

definitions.definition: "Director" or "Additional Director" or "Joint Director" means a Director or Additional Director or Joint Director, as the case may be, appointed under sub-section (1) of section 49 of this Act.
definitions.plain_english: A Joint Director is a senior government officer appointed by the Central Government to enforce the Prevention of Money Laundering Act. This officer holds a rank below the Director and Additional Director but above a Deputy Director. A Joint Director can be authorised to appoint lower-ranking officers and can exercise enforcement powers assigned under the Act.
real_world_examples: A Joint Director of the Enforcement Directorate (ED) in Mumbai leads an investigation into a real estate developer suspected of laundering proceeds from illegal hawala transactions through shell companies.

A Joint Director posted in Delhi is authorised by the Central Government to appoint Assistant Directors and other officers below the rank of Assistant Director to assist in money laundering cases involving cryptocurrency exchanges.

During a high-profile bank fraud case in Gujarat, a Joint Director issues summons to company executives and orders attachment of properties believed to be proceeds of crime under Chapter III of the Act.

A Joint Director in Chennai supervises the collection of evidence and coordinates with state police investigating a scheduled offence linked to drug trafficking, ensuring compliance with PMLA provisions.

A Joint Director in Kolkata reviews and approves search and seizure operations conducted by Deputy Directors against individuals suspected of layering funds through multiple bank accounts across different states.
what_it_covers: An officer appointed by the Central Government under sub-section (1) of section 49 to the rank of Joint Director for PMLA enforcement purposes.
A Joint Director who has been authorised to appoint authorities below the rank of Assistant Director under sub-section (2) of section 49.

A Joint Director exercising powers and discharging duties conferred under the Act, including investigation, attachment, and evidence collection, subject to conditions imposed by the Central Government.
A Joint Director functioning within the class of authorities listed under section 48, specifically in the first class alongside the Director and Additional Director.
what_it_excludes: A Deputy Director, who is a separately defined and lower-ranked authority appointed under the same section 49 but classified distinctly under section 48.
An Assistant Director, who is also appointed under section 49(1) but occupies a lower rank and has a separate definition under the Act.

Officers appointed by the Director, Additional Director, Joint Director, or Deputy Director under section 49(2), who are below the rank of Assistant Director and do not hold the designation of Joint Director.
Judicial or quasi-judicial officers such as the Adjudicating Authority or Members of the Appellate Tribunal, who are appointed under different provisions and serve distinct functions.
State government officers or police officials who may assist in PMLA investigations but are not appointed under section 49 and do not carry the statutory designation of Joint Director.
definitions.why_it_matters: The designation of Joint Director determines the scope of statutory powers an officer can exercise under the PMLA, including conducting investigations, issuing directions, attaching property, and delegating appointment authority to subordinate officers. Whether an action such as a search, summons, or attachment is legally valid may depend on whether it was carried out or authorised by an officer of the appropriate rank, making this definition critical to procedural legality under the Act.

definitions.definition: All proceedings before the Appellate Tribunal shall be deemed to be judicial proceedings within the meaning of sections 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (45 of 1860), thereby treating the Appellate Tribunal as a forum before which giving false evidence or causing obstruction constitutes a criminal offence.
definitions.plain_english: Judicial proceedings, in the context of this Act, means that hearings and procedures conducted before the Appellate Tribunal are treated the same as court proceedings for the purpose of certain criminal laws. This means that if someone lies under oath or misbehaves before the Tribunal, they can be prosecuted for perjury or contempt just as if they were in a regular court. This status gives the Tribunal's proceedings the weight and seriousness of formal court hearings.
real_world_examples: A witness summoned before the Appellate Tribunal in Mumbai in a money laundering appeal deliberately gives false testimony about financial transactions; because the proceedings are deemed judicial proceedings, he can be prosecuted under Section 193 IPC for giving false evidence.

A respondent's counsel in a Delhi Appellate Tribunal hearing intentionally insults and obstructs the Members during an ongoing appeal against an attachment order; this constitutes an offence under Section 228 IPC since the proceedings qualify as judicial proceedings.

A bank manager, while deposing before the Appellate Tribunal in a Kolkata hearing, fabricates documents related to suspicious transactions; the deemed judicial proceedings status allows the Tribunal to refer the matter for criminal prosecution under IPC provisions on false evidence.

A company director appears before the Appellate Tribunal in Chennai and wilfully provides incorrect affidavit evidence to obstruct the course of an attachment appeal; the judicial proceedings status enables law enforcement to register a perjury case against him.

During an ex parte hearing before the Appellate Tribunal in Hyderabad concerning proceeds of crime, an accused person's representative creates a disturbance to disrupt proceedings; the judicial proceedings classification ensures contempt-related criminal provisions under Sections 345 and 346 CrPC can be invoked.

An accused in a money laundering case attempts to bribe a witness outside the Appellate Tribunal chamber in Pune to alter testimony; because the proceedings are judicial in nature, this act of interference with judicial process attracts serious criminal liability.
what_it_covers: All hearings, examinations, and proceedings conducted before the Appellate Tribunal under the PMLA, which are deemed judicial proceedings for the purposes of Sections 193 and 228 of the IPC.
Any instance of a witness or party giving false evidence or making false statements on oath before the Appellate Tribunal, which becomes prosecutable as perjury under Section 193 IPC.
Acts of intentional insult or interruption to the Appellate Tribunal's proceedings, which are punishable under Section 228 IPC due to the judicial proceedings status.

Proceedings where the Appellate Tribunal exercises powers equivalent to a civil court, including summoning witnesses, requiring production of documents, and issuing commissions, all within the ambit of judicial proceedings.
what_it_excludes: Internal administrative or procedural decisions of the Appellate Tribunal that do not constitute a formal hearing or examination of parties, such as scheduling orders or registry-level processing.
Proceedings before the Adjudicating Authority, which is a separate forum under the PMLA and not expressly covered by the judicial proceedings deeming provision in Section 35.

Investigations or surveys conducted by enforcement authorities under the PMLA prior to the filing of an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal, as these are pre-adjudicatory and not tribunal proceedings.
Proceedings before civil courts or Special Courts under the PMLA, which derive their judicial character from their own statutory constitution and do not rely on the deeming fiction of Section 35.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of Appellate Tribunal proceedings as judicial proceedings is critical because it activates criminal penal provisions under Sections 193 and 228 of the IPC against any person who gives false evidence or causes obstruction, thereby deterring perjury and misconduct before the Tribunal. It also enables the Tribunal to function as a civil court under Sections 345 and 346 of the CrPC, ensuring that the integrity of money laundering adjudication is protected with the same force of law as regular court proceedings.

definitions.definition: A lease-hold interest, as used in Section 9 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, refers to any right, title, or interest in a property held by virtue of a lease, including any tenancy or occupancy right created by a lease agreement over immovable or movable property. Where the Adjudicating Authority finds that such a lease-hold interest has been created with a view to defeat the provisions of Chapter III (relating to attachment and confiscation), it may declare such lease-hold interest void, whereupon the property vests in the Central Government free from such interest.
definitions.plain_english: A lease-hold interest is the right a person gets to use or occupy someone else's property for a period of time under a lease or rental agreement. In the context of this law, it refers specifically to such rights that may have been created on a property that is being confiscated by the government due to money laundering. If the government authority believes the lease was created just to protect the property from confiscation, it can cancel that lease and take full ownership of the property.
real_world_examples: A money launderer who owns a commercial building in Mumbai, anticipating attachment, executes a 30-year lease in favour of a relative's shell company at a nominal rent just before the PMLA proceedings begin, hoping the lease will block the government from taking clean possession — the Adjudicating Authority can declare this lease-hold interest void under Section 9.

A person accused of money laundering creates a long-term agricultural lease over his farmland in Punjab in favour of a trusted associate for a token consideration of Re. 1 per year, to frustrate confiscation; the Adjudicating Authority, after hearing the lessee, finds the lease was a sham and nullifies the lease-hold interest so the land vests unencumbered in the Central Government.

A real estate developer in Hyderabad under PMLA investigation grants a 99-year leasehold right over a prime commercial property to an overseas entity controlled by family members, creating a lease-hold interest designed to complicate government acquisition; the authority can pierce this arrangement and void the interest.

A person involved in hawala transactions in Delhi transfers lease-hold interest in a warehouse to a nominee just days before the Enforcement Directorate attaches the property; the Adjudicating Authority determines the transfer was made to defeat confiscation and declares the lease-hold interest void, enabling the Central Government to take clear title.

In Chennai, a accused person creates a residential lease for a period of 50 years in favour of a benami entity over a luxury apartment attached under PMLA, attempting to encumber the property; upon hearing the lessee, the Adjudicating Authority finds the lease-hold interest was fraudulently created and cancels it so the property vests cleanly in the Central Government.
what_it_covers: A long-term lease of immovable property (residential, commercial, or agricultural) created by an accused person in favour of a relative, associate, or shell entity to frustrate confiscation under PMLA.
Any tenancy or occupancy right over attached or confiscated property that was granted after or just before PMLA proceedings commenced with the intent to encumber the property.
A leasehold interest created at a grossly undervalued consideration or for an unusually long duration that indicates it was designed to defeat the provisions of Chapter III of PMLA.
Lease-hold rights in movable or immovable property that survive formal attachment but are sought to be nullified by the Adjudicating Authority upon satisfaction that they were created mala fide.
what_it_excludes: A bona fide commercial lease entered into at fair market value well before any PMLA investigation or attachment proceedings were contemplated, where there is no intent to defeat confiscation.
Freehold ownership or absolute title held by the accused or any other person, which is governed separately as 'property' or 'encumbrance' under the Act rather than as a lease-hold interest.

A lease-hold interest held by a completely independent third party who had no knowledge of the money laundering activity and whose interest was not created to defeat confiscation — such a party retains the right to be heard and may have their interest protected.

Contractual rights that do not amount to a lease, such as a licence to use property or an easement right, which are distinct legal interests and do not constitute a lease-hold interest in the strict sense.
definitions.why_it_matters: If a lease-hold interest is found to have been created to defeat PMLA confiscation, the Adjudicating Authority can declare it void under Section 9, causing the property to vest absolutely and unencumbered in the Central Government; conversely, if the interest is genuine and not so created, the lessee retains enforceable rights and the Central Government takes the property subject to that interest. This determination directly affects whether the government obtains clean, encumbrance-free title and whether the accused's attempt to shield proceeds of crime through lease arrangements succeeds or fails.

Examples: A money launderer who owns a commercial building in Mumbai, anticipating attachment, executes a 30-year lease in favour of a relative's shell company at a nominal rent just before the PMLA proceedings begin, hoping the lease will block the government from taking clean possession — the Adjudicating Authority can declare this lease-hold interest void under Section 9. | A person accused of money laundering creates a long-term agricultural lease over his farmland in Punjab in favour of a trusted associate for a token consideration of Re. 1 per year, to frustrate confiscation; the Adjudicating Authority, after hearing the lessee, finds the lease was a sham and nullifies the lease-hold interest so the land vests unencumbered in the Central Government. | A real estate developer in Hyderabad under PMLA investigation grants a 99-year leasehold right over a prime commercial property to an overseas entity controlled by family members, creating a lease-hold interest designed to complicate government acquisition; the authority can pierce this arrangement and void the interest. | A person involved in hawala transactions in Delhi transfers lease-hold interest in a warehouse to a nominee just days before the Enforcement Directorate attaches the property; the Adjudicating Authority determines the transfer was made to defeat confiscation and declares the lease-hold interest void, enabling the Central Government to take clear title. | In Chennai, a accused person creates a residential lease for a period of 50 years in favour of a benami entity over a luxury apartment attached under PMLA, attempting to encumber the property; upon hearing the lessee, the Adjudicating Authority finds the lease-hold interest was fraudulently created and cancels it so the property vests cleanly in the Central Government.

definitions.definition: A 'legal representative' means any person who in law represents the estate of a deceased person, including heirs, executors, administrators, or any other person who is entitled to, or takes charge of, the property of a deceased person, for the purpose of continuing or preferring appeals arising out of proceedings under this Act in place of such deceased person.
definitions.plain_english: A legal representative is someone who steps into the shoes of a deceased person to continue or start legal proceedings on their behalf. When a person dies during a money laundering case, their legal heir or estate representative can carry on the appeal or legal fight in their place. This ensures that legal proceedings are not automatically terminated just because one party has passed away.
real_world_examples: A person whose property was attached under Section 8 of PMLA dies before filing an appeal with the Appellate Tribunal; his son, being the legal heir under Hindu succession law, steps in as legal representative to challenge the attachment order.

A woman accused in a money laundering case had filed an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal but dies of a heart attack during the pendency of the appeal; her husband, as legal representative, is permitted to continue the appeal in her place.

A businessman whose assets were frozen under PMLA is adjudicated insolvent and later dies; his daughter, who is his legal heir, approaches the High Court under Section 42 to continue the appeal originally filed by her father.

An executor named in the will of a deceased accused in a PMLA case applies to continue an ongoing appeal before the Appellate Tribunal, representing the estate of the deceased in accordance with Section 72.

A Delhi-based trader dies intestate during a PMLA proceeding; his widow and children collectively act as legal representatives and prefer a fresh appeal to the Appellate Tribunal under Section 72 within the prescribed limitation period.
what_it_covers: Legal heirs of the deceased (e.g., spouse, children, parents) who are entitled to represent the estate under personal law or succession law.
Executors or administrators of the estate of a deceased person appointed under a will or by a competent court.
Any person who lawfully takes charge of the property of the deceased and is recognized under law as capable of representing the estate in legal proceedings.
Persons authorized to prefer or continue appeals before the Appellate Tribunal or the High Court in place of the deceased under Section 72 of PMLA.
what_it_excludes: The official assignee or official receiver, who is separately mentioned in Section 72 and operates in cases of insolvency, not death, under separate insolvency legislation.
An authorised representative (such as a lawyer or power of attorney holder) acting on behalf of a living person, as that role is distinct from a legal representative representing a deceased's estate.
Creditors of the deceased who do not have a representative interest in the estate and have no legal standing to substitute as a party in proceedings under PMLA.
Strangers or third parties with no legal nexus to the deceased's estate, regardless of any financial or personal interest in the outcome of the proceedings.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of this definition determines whether an appeal or proceeding under PMLA can be continued after the death of the accused or affected party — without a recognized legal representative, the proceeding could lapse, potentially leaving an attachment order unchallenged or the estate unprotected. It directly governs the right to prefer or continue appeals under Sections 26 and 42 of the Act, ensuring that the death of a party does not result in an automatic denial of legal remedy to the estate.

definitions.definition: A letter of request is a formal judicial communication issued by the Special Court in India to a court or authority in a contracting State, or received by the Central Government from a court or authority in a contracting State, for the purpose of gathering evidence, executing attachment or confiscation orders, or otherwise facilitating mutual legal assistance in connection with investigation into an offence or proceedings under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act. Every such letter of request, along with any summons or warrant associated therewith, shall be transmitted or sent in such form and manner as the Central Government may, by notification, specify.
definitions.plain_english: A letter of request is an official written request sent by an Indian court to a foreign country's court or authority, or received from one, asking for help in a money laundering case. It can ask the foreign authority to collect evidence, examine facts, freeze or seize assets, or carry out other investigative steps. It works like a formal diplomatic and legal channel that allows courts in different countries to cooperate with each other in fighting financial crime.
real_world_examples: The Enforcement Directorate investigates a Mumbai-based hawala operator who has transferred proceeds of crime to bank accounts in Switzerland. The Special Court issues a letter of request to the Swiss Federal Criminal Court asking it to examine the account details, freeze the funds, and forward all documentary evidence to the Indian court.

A Delhi-based real estate company is found to have laundered money through shell companies in Mauritius. The Special Court, on an application by the Investigating Officer, issues a letter of request to the Mauritian Financial Intelligence Unit requesting examination of the shell company's directors and forwarding of financial records.

The Central Government receives a letter of request from a United Kingdom court seeking India's assistance in tracing and attaching property located in Hyderabad, which was acquired using proceeds of a fraud committed in the UK. The Central Government forwards the request to the Director of the Enforcement Directorate for execution under Indian law.

An NRI accused of money laundering has invested proceeds of crime in luxury apartments in Dubai. The Adjudicating Authority having confirmed attachment, the Special Court issues a letter of request to the Dubai courts requesting confiscation and repatriation of the property to India.

The Enforcement Directorate, during investigation of a cryptocurrency laundering network operating across India and Singapore, applies to the Special Court which issues a letter of request to the Singapore courts to examine blockchain transaction records and identify wallet holders connected to the Indian accused.
what_it_covers: Letters issued by the Special Court to a court or authority in a contracting State requesting examination of facts, collection of evidence, or execution of attachment and confiscation orders in money laundering investigations.

Letters received by the Central Government from a court or authority in a contracting State seeking India's assistance in tracing, attaching, or confiscating property within India derived from money laundering offences.
The transmission of summons and warrants alongside the letter of request between India and a contracting State in the prescribed form and manner notified by the Central Government.
All statements recorded, documents, or things received pursuant to a letter of request, which are deemed to be evidence collected during the course of investigation under the Act.
what_it_excludes: Requests made to or from non-contracting States, i.e., countries with which India has no bilateral or multilateral treaty or arrangement recognised under the PMLA, as such communications fall outside the scope of this provision.
Informal or diplomatic communications between governments not issued or directed through the Special Court or Central Government as prescribed under the Act.

Domestic summons, warrants, or judicial communications between courts within India, which are governed by the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and not by the letter of request mechanism under Chapter X of the PMLA.

Requests relating solely to tax matters, customs duties, or other fiscal offences not amounting to scheduled offences under the PMLA, which fall under separate bilateral tax information exchange agreements.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a communication qualifies as a letter of request under the PMLA determines whether evidence gathered abroad is admissible and deemed to be investigation evidence, and whether attachment or confiscation orders made by Indian authorities can be executed in foreign jurisdictions or vice versa; without this mechanism, cross-border money laundering prosecutions and asset recovery proceedings would stall entirely at national borders.
