definitions.definition: 'Member' means a Member of the Appellate Tribunal and includes the Chairperson.
definitions.plain_english: A 'Member' refers to any person who sits on the Appellate Tribunal under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, including the Chairperson of that Tribunal. In practice, this term also extends to members appointed to the Adjudicating Authority under Section 6. These are officially appointed individuals empowered to hear, adjudicate and decide cases related to money laundering and attachment of property.
real_world_examples: A retired High Court judge appointed to the Appellate Tribunal under PMLA hears an appeal filed by a real estate developer against an attachment order issued by the Enforcement Directorate — such a judge functions as a 'Member' of the Tribunal.

The Central Government appoints a senior IAS officer with finance background to serve on the Adjudicating Authority constituted under Section 6; this officer qualifies as a 'Member' for the purposes of adjudicating attachment proceedings.

A Bench of the Appellate Tribunal constituted by the Chairperson and two other Members sits in New Delhi to decide an appeal in a hawala money-laundering case involving a Mumbai-based trader — all sitting individuals, including the Chairperson, are 'Members' under the Act.

A person with experience in accountancy is appointed as one of the two Members of the Adjudicating Authority to assist in evaluating financial transactions in a complex bank fraud case involving proceeds of crime — this appointee is a 'Member' exercising statutory powers under the Act.

The Chairperson of the Appellate Tribunal, being a retired Supreme Court judge, presides over an appeal against a confiscation order; by explicit statutory inclusion, the Chairperson is also a 'Member' for all purposes under the Act.
what_it_covers: Any person formally appointed by the Central Government to serve as a Member of the Appellate Tribunal under the PMLA.
The Chairperson of the Appellate Tribunal, who is explicitly included within the definition of 'Member'.
Persons appointed as Members of the Adjudicating Authority under Section 6, including those with backgrounds in law, finance, accountancy, or administration.
A Member constituting a Bench of the Appellate Tribunal or Adjudicating Authority for the purpose of hearing and deciding cases.
what_it_excludes: Officers of the Enforcement Directorate such as the Director, Deputy Director, or Assistant Director, who exercise investigative powers but are not Members of the Tribunal or Adjudicating Authority.
Members of Parliament, members of State legislatures, or members of any other statutory body not constituted under PMLA — their membership in other bodies does not make them 'Members' under this Act.
Staff, registrars, or administrative personnel attached to the Appellate Tribunal or Adjudicating Authority who do not exercise adjudicatory powers.
Judges of the Special Court designated under Section 43, who exercise criminal jurisdiction separately from the Appellate Tribunal or Adjudicating Authority.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'Member' determines their authority to constitute a valid Bench, hear appeals or attachment proceedings, and pass binding orders under PMLA; any order passed by an improperly constituted body lacking a valid 'Member' is liable to be challenged as without jurisdiction. It also governs eligibility criteria, appointment procedures, service conditions, and protections against removal under Sections 30 and 31.

definitions.definition: 'Member' means a Member of the Appellate Tribunal and includes the Chairperson.
definitions.plain_english: A 'Member' under this law refers to any person who is officially appointed to sit on the Appellate Tribunal that hears appeals in money laundering cases. This includes not just the regular members but also the Chairperson who heads the Tribunal. In simple terms, it means any judge-like official who is part of the body that decides appeals against orders made under this law.
real_world_examples: A retired High Court judge appointed by the Central Government to serve on the Appellate Tribunal under PMLA hears an appeal filed by a businessman whose property was attached by the Enforcement Directorate — this judge is a 'Member' for the purposes of the Act.

The Chairperson of the Appellate Tribunal in New Delhi, presiding over a Bench hearing an appeal against an Adjudicating Authority's order confiscating proceeds of crime linked to a hawala network, is treated as a 'Member' under Section 2 of the PMLA.

An expert in finance or administration appointed to the Appellate Tribunal who participates in deciding an appeal by a non-banking financial company accused of facilitating money laundering qualifies as a 'Member' and exercises the powers described in Section 32 regarding resignation and removal.

When the Appellate Tribunal constitutes a Bench to hear an urgent appeal from a person whose bank accounts were frozen under PMLA, each official sitting on that Bench — including the Chairperson — is a 'Member' and their decisions carry the binding authority of the Tribunal.

A senior officer from the Indian Legal Service holding a Grade I post, appointed to the Appellate Tribunal to bring legal expertise to appeals involving complex offshore money laundering structures, functions as a 'Member' and is governed by service conditions applicable to Members under PMLA.
what_it_covers: Any person formally appointed by the Central Government to the Appellate Tribunal established under Section 25 of the PMLA, whether as a regular Member or in any designated capacity.
The Chairperson of the Appellate Tribunal, who is explicitly included within the definition of 'Member', thereby making all provisions applicable to Members equally applicable to the Chairperson.
A person qualified in the field of law, finance, administration, or accountancy who has been duly notified and seated as part of the Appellate Tribunal to adjudicate appeals arising under PMLA.
what_it_excludes: Members of the Adjudicating Authority appointed under Section 6, who form a separate body from the Appellate Tribunal and are not covered by this definition of 'Member'.
Officers of the Enforcement Directorate such as the Director, Deputy Director, or Assistant Director, who exercise investigative and enforcement powers but are not part of the Appellate Tribunal.

Advocates, legal representatives, or any authorised representatives appearing before the Appellate Tribunal on behalf of parties — they participate in proceedings but do not constitute 'Members' of the Tribunal.
Administrative staff, registrars, or support personnel working within the Appellate Tribunal who assist in its functioning but have not been appointed as Members in the statutory sense.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'Member' is critical because Section 32 governs the terms of resignation, removal, and service conditions specifically applicable to Members of the Appellate Tribunal — misidentifying who qualifies as a Member could affect the validity of tribunal proceedings, quorum requirements, and the enforceability of orders passed by the Appellate Tribunal. Only decisions made by duly constituted Members carry binding legal authority to confirm, modify, or set aside attachment and confiscation orders under PMLA.

definitions.definition: Money laundering is the process by which a person directly or indirectly attempts to indulge in, or knowingly assists or is a party to, or is actually involved in any process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime and projecting it as untainted property, as constituted under section 3 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. Properties involved in money laundering are subject to attachment, adjudication, and confiscation by the Central Government.
definitions.plain_english: Money laundering means taking money or property that was obtained through crime and making it appear as if it came from a legitimate source. It involves hiding the illegal origin of such funds by passing them through various transactions or businesses. Under Indian law, even attempting or knowingly helping someone do this is treated as the offence of money laundering.
real_world_examples: A Delhi-based real estate developer receives cash from drug traffickers and issues false sale deeds at inflated prices, converting black money into seemingly legitimate property assets registered with the Sub-Registrar.

A Mumbai hawala operator receives funds from fraudsters who have cheated PSU banks and routes the money through a chain of shell companies in Gujarat and Maharashtra, making the proceeds appear as legitimate business income.

A politician in Uttar Pradesh deposits large sums of bribery money in small tranches across multiple Jan Dhan accounts held by relatives, then consolidates the funds into a cooperative bank account to disguise the criminal origin — a practice known as structuring or smurfing.

A Hyderabad-based IT professional knowingly provides accounting services to a cybercrime syndicate, preparing books that show proceeds from phishing scams as software export revenue, thereby assisting in projecting tainted funds as untainted property.

A gold trader in Chennai purchases jewellery using proceeds from human trafficking and later sells it at market price through a legitimate showroom, converting criminal proceeds into clean cash with a valid GST invoice trail.

An NBFC promoter in Kolkata diverts loan funds sanctioned for a manufacturing unit into a network of fictitious vendors, cycles the money through multiple current accounts, and reinvests it in a luxury hotel project, laundering the proceeds of a banking fraud.
what_it_covers: Directly or indirectly dealing in, concealing, or converting proceeds of a scheduled offence to make them appear as legitimate income or property.

Knowingly assisting another person in any process or activity connected with proceeds of crime, including providing professional services such as accounting, legal structuring, or banking to disguise criminal funds.
Any attempt or actual involvement in projecting proceeds of crime as untainted property, including through shell companies, benami transactions, or layered financial transfers.
Property held by a third party on behalf of the accused that is traceable to the proceeds of a scheduled offence and declared involved in money laundering by the Adjudicating Authority.
International transfer of proceeds of crime to or from contracting States where reciprocal arrangements exist under section 59, making cross-border laundering schemes covered under this definition.
what_it_excludes: Legitimate income or assets that are acquired through lawful means and for which the accused can demonstrate a clean source, classified as untainted property under the Act.
Mere possession of property without knowledge of its criminal origin, as the offence requires knowing assistance or actual involvement in the process of laundering.

Transactions related to property not connected to any scheduled offence listed in the Schedule, since money laundering under this Act is necessarily linked to proceeds derived from a predicate scheduled offence.
Actions of a person acting in good faith without awareness that the funds or property involved were proceeds of crime, provided the good faith can be established on record.
Confiscated or forfeited property already vested in the Central Government, as such property no longer constitutes proceeds of crime available for laundering.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes money laundering under section 3 determines whether the accused faces rigorous imprisonment of three to seven years (extendable to ten years for scheduled offences under the NDPS Act) and unlimited fines under section 4, and triggers the burden of proof reversal under section 24 whereby the accused must prove the property is untainted. It also activates the Adjudicating Authority's power under section 8 to attach, adjudicate, and ultimately confiscate the properties declared involved in money laundering.

definitions.definition: 'Money-laundering' has the meaning assigned to it in section 3, which provides that whosoever directly or indirectly attempts to indulge or knowingly assists or knowingly is a party or is actually involved in any process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime and projecting it as untainted property shall be guilty of the offence of money-laundering.
definitions.plain_english: Money-laundering is the process by which money or property obtained through criminal activity is made to appear legitimate or 'clean'. This includes any direct or indirect attempt to handle, disguise, convert, or move such criminally derived money or property so that it looks like it came from a lawful source. Even knowingly helping someone else do this, or simply being a party to such activity, counts as money-laundering under Indian law.
real_world_examples: A politician in India receives bribes from a contractor and deposits the cash in small amounts across multiple bank accounts held by relatives, then uses those funds to purchase agricultural land registered in a family trust's name, effectively disguising the bribe money as legitimate family savings.

A drug trafficking syndicate operating in Mumbai converts its narcotics proceeds into gold jewellery through a network of complicit jewellers, then sells the jewellery through a legitimate retail shop to generate apparently clean sales revenue that is deposited into regular business accounts.

A Hawala operator in Delhi receives funds abroad generated from illegal arms deals and transfers equivalent amounts in India to designated recipients, with the funds appearing as legitimate remittances or loans in the books of a shell company registered in India.

A real estate developer in Bengaluru accepts large unaccounted cash payments from buyers for under-valued property registrations, books the excess cash as fictitious loans from related entities, and later writes off those loans as business losses, thereby laundering the proceeds of tax evasion.

An executive of a company involved in a financial fraud siphons funds into an overseas account and then routes the money back into India as Foreign Direct Investment through a layered chain of shell companies in Mauritius and Singapore, projecting the criminal proceeds as lawful foreign investment.
what_it_covers: Any direct or indirect attempt to indulge in any process or activity connected with proceeds of crime and projecting such proceeds as untainted property.
Knowingly assisting another person who is engaged in handling or concealing proceeds of a scheduled offence, even if the assistant did not commit the underlying crime.

Actual involvement in conversion, transfer, or integration of property derived from a scheduled offence, such as purchasing assets, routing funds through shell entities, or using hawala channels to project criminal proceeds as legitimate income.
Attempted money-laundering, meaning even an incomplete or unsuccessful effort to launder proceeds of crime attracts liability under the Act.
Being a knowing party to a money-laundering transaction, such as a chartered accountant or banker who is aware that funds being routed through their services represent proceeds of crime.
what_it_excludes: Handling or dealing with property that does not constitute 'proceeds of crime' as defined under the Act, i.e., property not derived from a scheduled offence, even if such dealings are otherwise irregular or tax non-compliant.
Innocent or bona fide transactions where the person involved had no knowledge that the property was derived from criminal activity relating to a scheduled offence.

Offences that do not appear in the Schedule to the Act — predicate offences not listed as scheduled offences cannot form the basis of a money-laundering charge, regardless of how the proceeds are handled.
Legitimate law enforcement actions such as attachment, seizure, or confiscation of proceeds of crime carried out by authorised authorities under the Act.
Civil or regulatory contraventions that do not amount to criminal activity under a scheduled offence, even where financial irregularities or misrepresentations are involved.

definitions.definition: 'Non-banking financial company' shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in clause (f) of section 45-I of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (2 of 1934).
definitions.plain_english: A non-banking financial company (NBFC) is a company registered under the Companies Act that provides financial services like loans, investments, and asset financing, but does not hold a banking licence and cannot accept demand deposits like a bank. These companies are regulated by the Reserve Bank of India. Examples include microfinance companies, gold loan companies, and housing finance companies that operate outside the traditional banking system.
real_world_examples: Bajaj Finance Limited, one of India's largest NBFCs, provides consumer loans, personal loans, and fixed deposits — if any of its transactions are suspected to involve proceeds of crime, PMLA obligations apply to it as an NBFC.

Muthoot Finance, a gold loan NBFC headquartered in Kerala, is required under PMLA to maintain KYC records and report suspicious transactions to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-IND) because it qualifies as an NBFC.

A microfinance institution (MFI) registered as an NBFC-MFI by RBI, operating in rural Jharkhand and providing small credit to women self-help groups, must comply with PMLA anti-money laundering obligations including record-keeping and reporting.

Shriram Transport Finance Company, an NBFC focused on commercial vehicle financing, was subject to PMLA scrutiny when certain loan transactions were flagged for potential layering of illicit funds through multiple loan accounts.

A chit fund company that is separately registered as an NBFC with RBI must comply with PMLA obligations in its capacity as an NBFC, distinct from its obligations as a chit fund company under the same Act.
what_it_covers: A company registered under the Companies Act and holding a Certificate of Registration from the RBI as an NBFC under section 45-IA of the RBI Act, 1934, engaged in lending or investment activities.

Asset finance companies, loan companies, investment companies, infrastructure finance companies, and microfinance institutions that meet the principal business criteria of financial activity as defined by RBI.
Gold loan companies such as Muthoot Finance or Manappuram Finance, which provide secured loans against gold jewellery and are registered NBFCs regulated by the RBI.
NBFC-Factors, NBFC-Peer-to-Peer Lending Platforms, and NBFC-Account Aggregators registered with RBI under respective master directions, all of which fall within the NBFC category for PMLA purposes.
what_it_excludes: Banking companies and co-operative banks, which are separately defined under the PMLA and governed by the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and are not classified as NBFCs.

Companies whose principal business is agriculture, industrial activity, purchase or sale of goods (other than securities), or providing services, as these do not meet the 'principal business' financial activity threshold prescribed by RBI for NBFC classification.
Housing finance institutions, which are separately defined and included within the definition of 'financial institution' under PMLA independently of the NBFC category, though some overlap may exist.

Insurance companies regulated by IRDAI and stock exchanges or intermediaries registered under SEBI, which are governed by separate regulatory frameworks and are not classified as NBFCs under the RBI Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a non-banking financial company determines whether it is treated as a 'financial institution' under PMLA, thereby triggering mandatory obligations including maintenance of records of transactions, verification of client identity, and reporting of suspicious transactions to FIU-IND. Failure to comply with these obligations by an NBFC can result in penalties, attachment of proceeds of crime, and prosecution under the PMLA.

It also encompasses, by extension, any scheduled offence whose proceeds form the predicate basis for a money-laundering charge.
definitions.plain_english: An 'offence' under this law means the crime of money laundering — that is, when someone takes money or property gained from illegal activity and tries to make it look like it came from a legal source. This includes anyone who helps, participates in, or is involved in such activity, even indirectly. Simply put, if you touch, move, hide, or disguise illegally obtained money or property, you have committed this offence.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based real estate developer accepts large cash payments from a drug trafficker and records them as legitimate property sales, thereby converting the proceeds of crime into apparently lawful assets — this constitutes the offence under Section 3.

A Delhi hawala operator receives funds linked to a terrorist financing network and transfers equivalent amounts to shell companies abroad, projecting the money as export proceeds — this qualifies as the offence of money-laundering.

A Bengaluru IT professional knowingly helps a fraudster layer stolen funds through multiple bank accounts and cryptocurrency wallets to obscure their origin — this person is guilty of the offence by virtue of knowingly assisting in the process.

A Chennai-based chartered accountant structures a series of fictitious loan transactions for a client whose funds originate from a corruption scandal, creating a paper trail that makes the proceeds appear as legitimate loan repayments — this amounts to the offence under the Act.

A Kolkata jeweller purchases high-value gold ornaments with cash payments received from a person involved in organised crime, knowing the source of funds, and later sells them to generate clean receipts — this constitutes participation in money-laundering activity.
what_it_covers: Directly or indirectly attempting to indulge in any process connected with proceeds of crime and projecting them as untainted property.
Knowingly assisting another person in laundering proceeds derived from a scheduled offence, even if the assistant did not commit the predicate offence.
Being actually involved in any activity — such as layering, integration, or placement — connected with the proceeds of a scheduled offence.
Persons who are a party to transactions designed to conceal the criminal origin of funds, including bank employees, lawyers, or accountants who knowingly facilitate such transactions.
Attempts to commit money-laundering, meaning even an incomplete or unsuccessful effort to project proceeds of crime as legitimate property is covered.
what_it_excludes: Offences that are not listed in the Schedule to the Act — a predicate crime that does not qualify as a scheduled offence cannot form the basis of a money-laundering offence under this Act.
Innocent or bona fide transactions where a person had no knowledge that the property involved was the proceeds of crime — lack of mens rea (guilty mind) excludes liability.
Offences specified under Part B of the Schedule where the total value involved is less than thirty lakh rupees, as these do not meet the threshold to qualify as scheduled offences.
Civil or regulatory contraventions, such as mere technical breaches of banking norms or FEMA violations, that do not involve the proceeds of a scheduled offence.
Acts committed by a person who is merely a victim of fraud or duress and had no voluntary participation or knowledge in the money-laundering activity.

definitions.definition: An 'offence under section 3' refers to the offence of money-laundering as defined under Section 3 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, which is committed by any person who directly or indirectly attempts to indulge or knowingly assists or knowingly is a party or is actually involved in any process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime and projecting it as untainted property. This offence forms the foundational predicate for triggering the Act's enforcement mechanisms, including survey, attachment, adjudication, and confiscation of property.
definitions.plain_english: An 'offence under section 3' simply means the crime of money laundering as defined in the PMLA. It is committed when a person deals with money or assets that were generated through criminal activity, tries to disguise or project that dirty money as clean or legitimate wealth. This is the core crime that the entire Prevention of Money Laundering Act is designed to detect, investigate, and punish.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based real estate developer knowingly purchases multiple properties using cash generated from drug trafficking proceeds, registering them in relatives' names to project the funds as legitimate rental income — this constitutes an offence under section 3.

A Hawala operator in Delhi receives money abroad from a terror-financing network and transfers equivalent amounts domestically through layered shell companies, thereby integrating proceeds of crime into the formal financial system — this amounts to an offence under section 3.

A bank manager in Chennai who is aware that a customer's large fixed deposits originate from fraudulent chit fund collections deliberately assists in structuring the deposits to avoid detection, making him knowingly party to an offence under section 3.

A Kolkata-based export firm inflates invoices for goods shipped abroad, repatriates excess foreign exchange, and invests it in stock markets through fictitious accounts — the process of layering and integration constitutes an offence under section 3.

A politician's family member in Hyderabad receives proceeds from a mining scam through a series of benami property purchases and projects rental yields from those properties as legitimate income, thereby committing an offence under section 3.

An accountant in Bengaluru knowingly prepares false books of accounts for a client to conceal proceeds derived from extortion, enabling the client to project illegal money as business profits — the accountant's knowing assistance constitutes an offence under section 3.
what_it_covers: Any direct or indirect attempt to indulge in a process or activity connected with proceeds of crime with intent to project them as untainted property.

Persons who knowingly assist, are knowingly party to, or are actually involved in any transaction or process involving proceeds of crime, including bankers, accountants, or lawyers who facilitate laundering with knowledge.
All acts of placement, layering, or integration of proceeds derived from a scheduled offence into the formal economy, whether through real estate, banking transactions, shell companies, or otherwise.
Situations where an authority has reason to believe such an offence has been committed, thereby enabling survey powers under Section 16 and adjudication proceedings under Section 8.
The reverse burden of proof under Section 24, whereby a person accused of this offence must prove that the proceeds of crime are untainted property.
what_it_excludes: The underlying scheduled offence (such as drug trafficking, corruption, or fraud) itself — the offence under section 3 is distinct from and additional to the predicate scheduled offence.

Innocent or bona fide transactions where the person dealing with the property had no knowledge or reason to believe that the funds constituted proceeds of crime, as good faith negates the 'knowingly' element.
Regulatory or technical contraventions of banking or financial regulations that do not involve proceeds of crime and are not connected to a scheduled offence listed in the PMLA Schedule.
Actions of a person who merely holds or transfers property under legal compulsion or court order without knowledge of its criminal origin.
Offences committed outside India where no element of the laundering process occurred within Indian jurisdiction and there is no nexus to proceeds of crime traceable in India.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person has committed or is reasonably believed to have committed an offence under section 3 is the foundational trigger for virtually all coercive powers under the PMLA, including survey under Section 16, provisional attachment under Section 5, adjudication proceedings under Section 8, and the imposition of penalty under Section 63. definitions.definition: An 'official assignee' means a person appointed under the Presidency-towns Insolvency Act, 1909 to whom the property of an insolvent debtor is assigned for the purpose of administration and distribution among creditors, and who, under section 72 of this Act, is empowered to prefer or continue an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal or the High Court in place of a person who has been adjudicated an insolvent, subject to the provisions of the applicable insolvency legislation.
definitions.plain_english: An official assignee is a court-appointed officer who takes over the financial affairs and property of a person who has been declared bankrupt (insolvent) in a Presidency town such as Mumbai, Kolkata, or Chennai. When such a bankrupt person has an ongoing legal case under the anti-money laundering law — such as a challenge to a property freeze order — the official assignee can step in and continue that case on their behalf. Essentially, this officer acts as the legal stand-in for the insolvent person to protect the interests of creditors in legal proceedings.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based businessman has his property attached under PMLA Section 8. He files an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal but is declared insolvent by a Presidency-towns court before the appeal concludes. The official assignee appointed by the Bombay insolvency court steps in to continue the appeal in his place.

A Kolkata trader whose assets were frozen under PMLA dies during the pendency of an appeal to the High Court under Section 42, and it is discovered he was also adjudicated insolvent. The official assignee, having jurisdiction over his estate, is authorised to continue the High Court appeal to contest the confiscation of assets that would otherwise go to creditors.

A Chennai textile company owner is adjudicated insolvent under the Presidency-towns Insolvency Act before he could file an appeal against an Appellate Tribunal order confirming attachment of his property. The official assignee files a fresh appeal before the High Court under Section 42 of PMLA in his place, arguing that the attached property should be released to satisfy legitimate creditor claims.

An insolvent individual in Mumbai had multiple bank accounts frozen by the Enforcement Directorate under PMLA. After adjudication of insolvency, the official assignee, acting under Section 72(3) read with the Presidency-towns Insolvency Act 1909, exercises the right to challenge the attachment order before the Appellate Tribunal to recover unencumbered assets for distribution to creditors.

A real estate developer in Kolkata adjudicated insolvent while an Appellate Tribunal hearing on attached property is ongoing. The official assignee evaluates the merit of the PMLA proceedings and decides to continue the appeal, as a successful outcome could free up assets worth crores for creditor distribution.
what_it_covers: An officer appointed under the Presidency-towns Insolvency Act, 1909 to administer the estate of a person adjudicated insolvent in Mumbai, Kolkata, or Chennai.
The right to prefer or continue an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal against a property attachment order under PMLA when the original party has been adjudicated insolvent.
The right to prefer or continue an appeal before the High Court under Section 42 of PMLA when the person entitled to appeal has been adjudicated insolvent.
Exercise of powers subject to the constraints and framework of the Presidency-towns Insolvency Act, 1909, as mandated under Section 72(3) of PMLA.
what_it_excludes: An official receiver appointed under the Provincial Insolvency Act, 1920, who operates in non-Presidency town jurisdictions and is treated as a separate functionary under Section 72.
Legal representatives such as heirs or executors of a deceased person, who are governed separately under Section 72 as a distinct category of substitute litigants.
Liquidators appointed under the Companies Act or Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, who are not designated as 'official assignees' under the Presidency-towns Insolvency Act, 1909.
A private trustee or contractual assignee appointed by the insolvent person voluntarily, who does not hold the statutory designation of 'official assignee' under the applicable insolvency law.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of this definition determines whether a PMLA appeal against property attachment or confiscation can survive the insolvency of the accused — if the official assignee qualifies and steps in, the proceedings continue and the outcome may affect the pool of assets available to creditors; failure to recognise this role could result in unchallenged forfeiture of assets that would otherwise satisfy creditor claims. It directly governs the locus standi of the official assignee to appear before the Appellate Tribunal and the High Court under Sections 26 and 42 of PMLA.

The Appellate Tribunal rules against him and he seeks to appeal before the High Court, but is adjudicated insolvent before filing. definitions.definition: 'Person' includes an individual, a Hindu undivided family, a company, a firm, an association of persons or a body of individuals, whether incorporated or not, every artificial juridical person not falling within any of the preceding sub-clauses, and any agency, office or branch owned or controlled by any of the above persons mentioned in the preceding sub-clauses.
definitions.plain_english: A 'person' under this law is not limited to a human being. It covers a wide range of entities — from individual humans to families, companies, firms, clubs, trusts, and even foreign branches or offices controlled by any of these entities. Essentially, anyone or any organisation that can hold property, conduct transactions, or be held legally responsible can qualify as a 'person' under this Act.
real_world_examples: An individual Mumbai-based real estate broker who launders proceeds from drug trafficking by purchasing property in his own name is a 'person' liable under the Act.
A private limited company registered in Delhi whose directors route kickbacks from government contracts through shell accounts is treated as a 'person' and its assets can be attached.
A Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) in Rajasthan that collectively invests proceeds of a scheduled offence in agricultural land qualifies as a 'person' subject to investigation and attachment proceedings.

A partnership firm in Surat operating in the textile trade that is found to have layered proceeds of crime through fictitious trade invoices is a 'person' against whom money-laundering charges can be brought.

The Indian branch of a foreign bank, being an agency or office owned or controlled by a foreign entity, is considered a 'person' and can be investigated if it facilitates placement of proceeds of crime.
An unregistered association of traders in Hyderabad collectively holding undisclosed proceeds from hawala transactions constitutes a 'body of individuals' and thus a 'person' under the Act.
what_it_covers: An individual Indian citizen or foreign national who commits or benefits from a scheduled offence.
A Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) that collectively holds or transfers proceeds of crime.
A company incorporated under the Companies Act, whether public or private, involved in layering or integration of laundered funds.
A firm — whether registered or unregistered partnership — used as a vehicle for placement of illegal proceeds.
An association of persons or body of individuals (e.g., a club, society, or trade association), whether incorporated or not, found to be holding proceeds of crime.
Any artificial juridical person such as a statutory body or government undertaking not covered by the other sub-clauses.
Any agency, office, or branch owned or controlled by any of the above, including Indian branches of foreign corporations.
what_it_excludes: A deceased individual's estate acting independently — the definition does not extend to an estate in its own right unless represented by a legal representative recognised under the Act.
A sovereign foreign government acting in its official governmental capacity is generally not within the contemplation of this definition as a 'person' subject to domestic prosecution.
An unborn child or foetus, which has no legal personality and cannot hold property or be a party to transactions under Indian law.
A court or judicial authority constituted under law, which acts as a public institution rather than a legal person for purposes of this Act.
Entities that are merely incidental intermediaries with no ownership or control link to the persons defined — e.g., an independent clearing house with no stake in the transaction.
definitions.why_it_matters: The scope of who qualifies as a 'person' directly determines who can be investigated, prosecuted, and whose property can be provisionally attached or confiscated under Chapters III and IV of the Act; if an entity falls outside this definition, the authorities cannot initiate attachment, freezing, or criminal proceedings against it under PMLA. It also triggers compliance obligations such as KYC, record-keeping, and reporting duties for reporting entities dealing with such persons.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of sub-section (4) of section 5, 'person interested', in relation to any immovable property, includes all persons claiming or entitled to claim any interest in the property.
definitions.plain_english: A 'person interested' is anyone who has a claim or a right to claim some interest in an immovable property that has been provisionally attached under the money laundering law. This could be an owner, a co-owner, a tenant, a mortgagee, or anyone else who legally holds or can assert a stake in that property. The law protects such a person's right to continue enjoying the property even while it is under provisional attachment.
real_world_examples: A co-owner of a flat in Mumbai whose property is provisionally attached because his business partner is accused of money laundering — the co-owner is a 'person interested' and retains the right to enjoy his share of the property during attachment.

A tenant living in a Delhi house that has been attached under PMLA continues to be a 'person interested' as he holds a valid lease agreement and cannot be evicted merely because the property is provisionally attached.
A bank that holds a mortgage over a Bengaluru commercial property attached under PMLA is a 'person interested' since it has a financial claim (encumbrance) over the property.

A widow who inherited a share of agricultural land in Punjab that was subsequently attached due to her son's alleged money laundering offence qualifies as a 'person interested' and can assert her right to enjoy that portion of land.

A developer who has entered into an agreement to sell with a buyer for a Chennai apartment, and has received partial consideration, may be a 'person interested' if the property is attached, as they retain contractual rights over the property.

A Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) member who has a right by birth in a jointly held property attached under PMLA is a 'person interested' entitled to protect their interest before the Adjudicating Authority.
what_it_covers: A co-owner or joint owner of the attached immovable property who holds a registered share in it.
A mortgagee or creditor who holds a charge or encumbrance over the attached immovable property as security for a loan.
A tenant or lessee with a valid lease agreement over the attached immovable property who has a possessory interest.
Legal heirs or successors who have inherited or are entitled to inherit a share in the attached immovable property.
A person who has entered into a registered agreement to purchase the immovable property and has part-paid consideration, giving rise to an equitable interest.
what_it_excludes: Persons who have no legal or equitable claim over the immovable property and are merely in physical occupation without any title or agreement.

Persons whose purported interest in the property was created specifically to defeat the provisions of PMLA confiscation, as such interests can be declared void by the Adjudicating Authority under section 9.

Movable property holders — the definition is explicitly limited to immovable property under section 5(4), so holders of interests in attached movable property do not fall under this specific definition.
A person whose claimed interest arises solely from an unregistered and legally unenforceable document that does not create any recognizable right in the property.
Third parties who are merely related to or associated with the accused but hold no independent legal, contractual, or equitable interest in the specific immovable property in question.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a person as a 'person interested' under section 5 determines who is entitled to continue enjoying an immovable property despite its provisional attachment, thereby safeguarding innocent third-party rights during the attachment period. It is also relevant under section 9, where the Adjudicating Authority must give such persons an opportunity of being heard before confiscation, which can affect whether encumbrances or leasehold interests are voided and title vests absolutely in the Central Government.

definitions.definition: The term 'prescribed value' refers to the monetary threshold of transactions, as may be prescribed by rules made under this Act, below which a transaction or series of integrally connected transactions may be structured so as to evade the reporting obligations under Section 12; the principal officer of a banking company, financial institution, or intermediary is obligated to report transactions deliberately kept below this value to the Director when there is reason to believe such structuring is intended to defeat the provisions of Section 12.
definitions.plain_english: The 'prescribed value' is a specific rupee amount set by government rules that acts as a trigger for mandatory reporting of financial transactions by banks and other financial entities. If a transaction equals or exceeds this amount, it must be reported to the anti-money laundering authority. The rule also covers situations where someone intentionally breaks up a large transaction into smaller ones to stay below this threshold and avoid detection.
real_world_examples: A customer at a State Bank of India branch makes 10 separate cash deposits of ₹9,500 each on the same day, all kept just below the prescribed reporting threshold, to avoid triggering the bank's mandatory reporting obligation to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-IND).

A Kolkata-based jeweller conducts multiple gold purchase transactions with different employees of the same company within a single month, each slightly below the prescribed value, in what appears to be a deliberate attempt to evade Section 12 reporting requirements.

An NBFC (Non-Banking Financial Company) registered in Mumbai receives a series of loan repayments from a single borrower on consecutive days, each fractionally below the prescribed value; the principal officer, suspecting structuring, reports the series to the Director as an inter-connected transaction.

A cooperative bank in Pune notices a customer splitting a ₹20 lakh property-related payment into multiple transactions of ₹1.9 lakh each over a month; the bank's compliance officer flags this as deliberate structuring below the prescribed value and files a Suspicious Transaction Report with FIU-IND.

An online payment intermediary (fintech platform) detects a merchant conducting 50 transactions per day all capped at just below the prescribed value threshold across different accounts linked to the same PAN, prompting the principal officer to report the pattern to the Director.
what_it_covers: The minimum monetary value of a single transaction that must be reported by banking companies, financial institutions, and intermediaries to the Director under Section 12.
A series of integrally connected transactions within a month that collectively meet or exceed the prescribed value, even if each individual transaction is below the threshold.

Transactions deliberately structured or split by a customer to remain below the prescribed value with the intent to defeat the reporting requirements of Section 12, which the principal officer must still report upon forming a belief of such intent.
Both cash and non-cash transactions whose nature and value are prescribed by the government rules, requiring maintenance of records by regulated entities.
what_it_excludes: Transactions whose aggregate or individual value is genuinely and incidentally below the prescribed threshold without any intent to evade reporting obligations, which do not trigger the mandatory reporting duty.

Transactions between parties who are not clients of banking companies, financial institutions, or intermediaries, as the prescribed value obligation applies only within the context of these regulated entities.
Internal fund transfers or inter-bank settlement transactions that are not client-originated and do not fall within the nature of transactions prescribed under the rules.
Transactions that fall outside the prescribed categories of nature and type as specified in the rules, even if their value exceeds the threshold amount.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a transaction meets or is deliberately kept below the prescribed value determines whether a banking company, financial institution, or intermediary is legally obligated to report it to the Director, thereby triggering the anti-money laundering surveillance mechanism under the PMLA. Failure to report transactions at or above this value, or transactions suspected to be structured below it, exposes the principal officer and the institution to penalties and prosecution under the Act.

definitions.definition: The principal officer of a banking company, financial institution, or intermediary is the designated senior official who bears the responsibility of identifying suspicious transactions and furnishing information regarding single transactions or series of transactions that appear to have been valued below the prescribed threshold so as to defeat the provisions of Section 12, and reporting such transactions to the Director within the prescribed time.
definitions.plain_english: The principal officer is the designated senior official within a bank, financial institution, or intermediary who is responsible for monitoring transactions and reporting suspicious activity to the government authority known as the Director. This person has the duty to spot transactions that seem to have been deliberately broken into smaller amounts to avoid detection. They must report such suspicious transactions within the time period set by law.
real_world_examples: The Chief Compliance Officer of State Bank of India notices that a customer has conducted multiple cash deposits of Rs. 4.9 lakh each on consecutive days — just below the Rs. 5 lakh reporting threshold — and as the principal officer, she files a suspicious transaction report with the Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-IND).

At a Mumbai-based stock broking firm registered as an intermediary under SEBI, the designated principal officer observes a series of securities trades that appear structured to avoid the prescribed transaction value limits, and accordingly furnishes details of those trades to the Director within the prescribed timeline.

A senior compliance manager of a Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) in Bengaluru, acting as principal officer, identifies that a borrower has repaid loans in multiple small tranches across several branches in a single month to stay below reporting thresholds, and submits the requisite information to the FIU-IND.

The principal officer of a private sector bank in Delhi reviews a series of foreign remittance transactions by a single client that are each just under the prescribed limit, reasons that they are integrally connected and structured to evade Section 12, and reports them to the Director within the prescribed period.

At a chit fund company operating in Chennai, the designated principal officer discovers that a member has been making cash payments through multiple accounts in a coordinated manner to defeat the reporting obligations, and immediately furnishes the transaction information to the Director as required under the proviso to Section 12(1).
what_it_covers: A designated senior compliance officer of a banking company who has the authority and responsibility to identify and report suspicious or structured transactions to the Director.

A senior official of a financial institution or intermediary who has reason to believe that transactions have been deliberately valued below the prescribed threshold to evade reporting requirements under Section 12.

The Chief Compliance Officer or equivalent designated person in an NBFC, housing finance institution, or stock broker registered as an intermediary, who is tasked with fulfilling the reporting obligations under the PMLA.

Any officer formally designated by the banking company, financial institution, or intermediary to discharge the statutory duty of furnishing transaction information to the Director within the prescribed time.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary bank employees or tellers who handle transactions on a day-to-day basis but are not designated with the specific compliance and reporting responsibilities under PMLA.

External auditors or statutory auditors of a banking company or financial institution, who may review records but do not hold the designated authority to report transactions to the Director under Section 12.
The Director of the Financial Intelligence Unit himself, who is the recipient of the reports rather than the person obligated to furnish them under Section 12.
Customers or clients of the banking company or financial institution, who are the subjects of verification and record-keeping but bear no reporting obligation as principal officers.
Board members or directors of a banking company who do not hold a specific designation as the principal officer responsible for PMLA compliance and reporting.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identification of the principal officer is critical because it is this specific individual who bears the legal duty under Section 12 to furnish suspicious transaction information to the Director, and failure to do so can attract prosecution and penalties under the PMLA. If no principal officer is properly designated or if the designated officer fails to report structured or suspicious transactions, the banking company, financial institution, or intermediary itself may face regulatory and criminal liability for non-compliance with PMLA obligations.

definitions.definition: The term 'proceeding' is not expressly defined in Section 2 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002; however, as used in Section 50 and throughout the Act, it means any inquiry, investigation, hearing, adjudication, or other formal process conducted under the authority of the Act before the Director, Adjudicating Authority, Appellate Tribunal, or Special Court, including proceedings for the purpose of collecting evidence, summoning persons, or determining attachment, confiscation, or liability for money laundering. Such a proceeding is deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of sections 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code.
definitions.plain_english: A 'proceeding' under this law refers to any official legal process or hearing that takes place under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, whether it is an investigation, an inquiry before an officer, or a formal hearing before a tribunal or court. When someone is called to appear, submit documents, or give evidence as part of a money laundering inquiry, that entire process is called a 'proceeding.' Importantly, such proceedings carry the same weight as court proceedings, meaning lying or refusing to cooperate can lead to criminal consequences.
real_world_examples: The Enforcement Directorate issues a summons to the CFO of a Mumbai-based real estate company under Section 50, directing him to appear before the Deputy Director and produce financial records related to suspected layering of proceeds from fraud — this formal inquiry constitutes a 'proceeding' under the Act.

The Adjudicating Authority in New Delhi conducts a hearing to determine whether properties attached by the ED in a hawala money laundering case should be confirmed for confiscation — the entire hearing process before the Adjudicating Authority is a 'proceeding.'

A witness summoned by the Director of Enforcement to depose in connection with a scheduled offence committed by a Kolkata-based shell company network appears before the authority to record a statement — this examination on oath is a 'proceeding' deemed judicial under the IPC.

The Appellate Tribunal hears an appeal filed by a person aggrieved by an attachment order passed by the Adjudicating Authority in a case involving proceeds of crime linked to drug trafficking in Punjab — the appeal hearing before the Tribunal is a 'proceeding' under the Act.

An Enforcement Officer conducts a survey and calls upon the principal officer of a Chennai cooperative bank to furnish account statements and transaction records as part of an inquiry into suspected money laundering — the survey and inquiry together constitute a 'proceeding' under the Act.

The Special Court in Hyderabad takes cognizance of a complaint filed by the ED against accused persons for the offence of money laundering under Section 3, and conducts trial proceedings — each stage of the trial is a 'proceeding' under the Act.
what_it_covers: Inquiries and examinations conducted by the Director or Deputy Director under Section 50 for summoning persons and collecting evidence related to money laundering.
Hearings before the Adjudicating Authority for confirming, revoking, or adjudicating provisional attachment orders under Chapter III of the Act.
Proceedings before the Appellate Tribunal arising from appeals against orders of the Adjudicating Authority or other authorities under the Act.
Trial proceedings before the Special Court designated under Section 43 for offences of money laundering under Section 3.
Any formal process before an authorised officer of the Central Government under the Act for the collection of evidence, recording of statements, or production of documents.
what_it_excludes: Internal administrative or departmental inquiries conducted by government agencies or departments not acting under the authority of the PMLA.
Civil suits or proceedings before ordinary civil courts filed independently of the PMLA framework, such as recovery suits or property disputes not connected to money laundering.
Criminal proceedings in regular courts for the predicate scheduled offence itself (e.g., a trial under the IPC for fraud), which are separate from PMLA proceedings.
Parliamentary or legislative committee inquiries or investigations, which are not conducted under the authority of the PMLA.
Informal inquiries, preliminary fact-finding exercises, or internal bank investigations conducted by reporting entities under their own compliance frameworks.
definitions.why_it_matters: The characterisation of an inquiry or hearing as a 'proceeding' under the PMLA is critical because it triggers the deeming fiction in Section 50(4) that treats the proceeding as a judicial proceeding under Sections 193 and 228 of the IPC, thereby making false statements, perjury, or obstruction punishable as criminal offences. It also determines the scope of the Director's coercive powers to summon persons, compel production of records, and enforce attendance, and governs the evidentiary value of statements recorded during such proceedings.

definitions.definition: 'Proceeds of crime' means any property derived or obtained, directly or indirectly, by any person as a result of criminal activity relating to a scheduled offence or the value of any such property.
definitions.plain_english: Proceeds of crime refers to any property or money that a person gains, directly or through a chain of transactions, because of committing a serious criminal offence listed in the Schedule of the Act. It also includes the monetary value of such property even if the property itself is no longer traceable. Essentially, it is the 'profit' or 'benefit' arising from crime.
real_world_examples: A drug trafficker in Mumbai sells narcotics and deposits the cash earnings into a bank account — the cash deposited constitutes proceeds of crime as it was obtained from a scheduled narcotic offence.

A government official in Delhi accepts bribes in exchange for awarding public contracts; the bribe money and any assets purchased with it (such as a flat in Noida) are proceeds of crime derived from the corruption offence.

A fraudster in Bengaluru runs a Ponzi scheme, collects crores from investors, and converts the money into gold jewellery — both the collected funds and the jewellery are proceeds of crime relating to the scheduled cheating/fraud offence.

A wildlife poacher in Madhya Pradesh sells tiger skins illegally and uses the proceeds to buy agricultural land in his wife's name — the land represents proceeds of crime derived indirectly from the wildlife-related scheduled offence.

A hawala operator in Hyderabad receives foreign funds generated from terrorist financing activities abroad and converts them into Indian rupees — the rupee equivalent constitutes proceeds of crime linked to the scheduled terror-financing offence.

A company director in Chennai siphons funds from his firm through fictitious invoices into a shell company and then buys luxury cars — those cars are proceeds of crime obtained indirectly from a scheduled corporate fraud offence.
what_it_covers: Cash, bank deposits, or digital money directly received as payment or reward for committing a scheduled offence such as drug trafficking or corruption.
Property purchased, invested in, or acquired using money generated from a scheduled offence, even through multiple layers of transactions (indirect proceeds).
The fair market value of proceeds of crime where the original property has been dissipated, consumed, transferred, or cannot be located — allowing authorities to pursue equivalent value assets.
Property held in the name of a third party (such as a family member or associate) if it was derived or obtained as a result of the accused's criminal activity relating to a scheduled offence.
Foreign assets or property located outside India that were obtained by any person as a result of criminal activity relating to a scheduled offence committed in India.
what_it_excludes: Legitimate income, salary, business profits, or property acquired entirely independent of any scheduled offence, even if the owner is otherwise involved in criminal activity.
Property derived from an offence that does not fall within the Schedule to the PMLA — crimes not listed as scheduled offences cannot generate 'proceeds of crime' for PMLA purposes.
Untainted property — property that has not been derived or obtained, directly or indirectly, from any criminal activity relating to a scheduled offence is explicitly outside this definition.

Proceeds arising solely from offences under Part B of the Schedule where the total value involved is less than thirty lakh rupees, as such offences do not qualify as scheduled offences under those circumstances.
Restitution amounts or compensation paid by a court to a victim out of general government funds, as these are not 'derived or obtained' by any person as a result of criminal activity.
definitions.why_it_matters: The entire liability for the offence of money-laundering under Section 3 and the punishment under Section 4 are contingent on whether the property in question qualifies as 'proceeds of crime' — without this nexus to a scheduled offence, no PMLA prosecution, attachment under Section 5, search and seizure under Sections 16–18, or confiscation can be validly initiated. It also governs the presumption under Section 24, which reverses the burden of proof onto the accused once proceeds of crime are established.

definitions.definition: 'property' means any property or assets of every description, whether corporeal or incorporeal, movable or immovable, tangible or intangible and includes deeds and instruments evidencing title to, or interest in, such property or assets, wherever located.
definitions.plain_english: Property under this law means absolutely anything of value that a person can own or have an interest in — whether it is something physical like land, cash, or jewellery, or something non-physical like a bank account, shares, or intellectual property rights. It also includes the legal documents that prove ownership of or interest in any such asset. It does not matter where in the world the property is located.
real_world_examples: A politician in Mumbai purchases multiple residential flats using cash generated from bribery. These flats, being immovable physical assets, qualify as 'property' under PMLA and are liable to provisional attachment by the Enforcement Directorate.

A Delhi-based businessman routes hawala money through shell companies and acquires shares in a listed Indian company. Those shareholdings, being incorporeal and intangible assets, fall within the definition of 'property' and can be seized under the Act.

A drug trafficker in Punjab deposits proceeds of narcotics sales into a savings bank account and then moves funds into fixed deposits. The bank account balances and fixed deposit receipts constitute 'property' susceptible to attachment under Section 5 of PMLA.

A Kolkata jeweller converts black money into gold bullion and diamond jewellery. Both the physical jewellery (tangible movable property) and any title deeds or invoices evidencing ownership are covered as 'property' under PMLA.

A Bengaluru-based fraudster registers a patent using funds derived from a Ponzi scheme. The intellectual property rights in the patent, being intangible incorporeal property, fall squarely within the PMLA definition and can be attached and confiscated.

A Mumbai real estate developer accepts unaccounted cash and creates a mortgage or lease deed in favour of a benamidar. The lease-hold interest and the deed itself are explicitly covered as 'property' since the definition includes instruments evidencing interest in assets.
what_it_covers: Immovable physical assets such as land, residential flats, commercial buildings and agricultural property registered in India or abroad.
Movable tangible assets including cash, gold, jewellery, vehicles, machinery and artwork.
Intangible incorporeal assets such as bank account balances, fixed deposits, shares, mutual fund units, bonds, derivatives and cryptocurrency holdings.
Intellectual property rights including patents, trademarks, copyrights and design rights acquired using proceeds of crime.
Legal documents and instruments such as sale deeds, mortgage deeds, share certificates and title papers that evidence ownership of or interest in any asset.
Assets located outside India, given the explicit 'wherever located' language in the definition.
what_it_excludes: Personal services or labour — a person's skill, time or contractual obligations to perform work do not constitute 'property' under this definition.
Purely contingent or unaccrued future rights that have no present recognisable value and cannot be evidenced by any deed or instrument.
Untainted property that has no nexus whatsoever to any scheduled offence or criminal activity, as the operative provisions of PMLA are triggered only in relation to proceeds of crime.
Reputational interests, goodwill not separately assignable or evidenced, and other purely personal non-transferable rights.
Penal fines or penalties imposed by a court, which represent State obligations rather than assets owned by a person.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of this definition is the threshold condition for almost every enforcement action under PMLA — attachment under Section 5, adjudication under Section 8, and confiscation under Section 9 all operate on 'property', so whether an asset qualifies as 'property' directly determines whether it can be seized, frozen, or permanently confiscated by the State. If an item falls outside this definition, the Enforcement Directorate loses jurisdiction to attach or confiscate it, and the accused cannot be prosecuted for laundering that item.

definitions.definition: A Public Prosecutor, for the purposes of this Act, means a person appointed to conduct prosecution before a Special Court under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, who is deemed to be a Public Prosecutor within the meaning of clause (u) of section 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973; such person must have been in practice as an advocate for not less than seven years under the Union or a State requiring special knowledge of law. The Central Government may also appoint a Special Public Prosecutor for any case or class or group of cases.
definitions.plain_english: A Public Prosecutor under the PMLA is a senior lawyer appointed by the government to represent the state and argue cases in the Special Court that handles money laundering matters. They must have at least seven years of experience as an advocate. Their role includes opposing bail applications for accused persons and conducting the trial on behalf of the prosecution.
real_world_examples: The Central Government appoints a senior advocate with over ten years of experience as a Special Public Prosecutor to conduct the prosecution in the high-profile hawala money laundering case before the Special PMLA Court in New Delhi.

In a case involving proceeds of crime linked to a real estate scam in Mumbai, the Public Prosecutor appears before the Special Court to oppose the bail application of the accused developer, arguing that he is likely to tamper with evidence if released.

The Enforcement Directorate files a complaint before the Special Court in Chennai against a chit fund operator accused of money laundering; the designated Public Prosecutor conducts examination of witnesses and cross-examines the defence's witnesses throughout the trial.

A person convicted under Section 4 of the PMLA appeals before the High Court; the Public Prosecutor who conducted the original prosecution before the Special Court is called upon to assist the government in defending the conviction.

In a terror-financing linked money laundering case in Hyderabad, the Central Government appoints a Special Public Prosecutor with expertise in financial crimes specifically for that case to ensure skilled representation given its complexity.

During a bail hearing at the Special Court in Kolkata for an accused in a bank fraud-linked money laundering case, the Public Prosecutor presents detailed arguments on why there are no reasonable grounds to believe the accused is innocent, thereby satisfying the twin conditions under Section 45.
what_it_covers: A lawyer appointed by the Central Government to conduct prosecution before the PMLA Special Court, having at least seven years of practice as an advocate.
A Special Public Prosecutor appointed by the Central Government for a specific case or class or group of cases before the Special Court.

Any person conducting prosecution before the Special Court, who is deemed by law to be a Public Prosecutor within the meaning of clause (u) of Section 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, with all attendant rights and duties under the CrPC.
what_it_excludes: Any advocate with less than seven years of practice, who does not meet the statutory qualification requirement for appointment as Public Prosecutor or Special Public Prosecutor under Section 46.
Police officers or Enforcement Directorate officers who investigate money laundering offences — they perform investigative functions and are not covered by the role of Public Prosecutor.
Private lawyers engaged by the accused or complainants in a personal capacity, who appear on behalf of private parties and not on behalf of the state or the prosecution.

Officers of the Central Government or State Government who file written complaints to initiate cognizance under Section 45, as they perform a complainant function and are not prosecutors conducting the trial.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence and role of the Public Prosecutor is a mandatory prerequisite for bail decisions under Section 45 — no accused can be released on bail for offences punishable with more than three years under Part A of the Schedule unless the Public Prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose the application, making their participation a statutory safeguard. Additionally, the appointment of a qualified Public Prosecutor ensures lawful conduct of prosecution before the Special Court, and any defect in such appointment may affect the validity of the proceedings.

definitions.definition: The Chairperson, Members and other officers and employees of the Appellate Tribunal, the Adjudicating Authority, Director and the officers subordinate to him shall be deemed to be public servants within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (45 of 1860).
definitions.plain_english: Certain key officials involved in enforcing the Prevention of Money Laundering Act — such as members of the Appellate Tribunal, the Adjudicating Authority, the Director, and their staff — are treated as government public servants under Indian law. This means they are bound by the duties and held to the standards expected of public servants, and any misconduct or bribery involving them attracts the same criminal consequences as if they were regular government officials. This designation is a legal fiction created by the Act to ensure accountability.
real_world_examples: The Director of the Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-IND), while conducting an investigation into a hawala network, is considered a public servant; if someone offers him a bribe to drop the case, the briber can be prosecuted under IPC sections related to bribing a public servant.

An officer of the Adjudicating Authority in Mumbai who deliberately delays an attachment order in exchange for a payment from the accused would be liable for criminal misconduct as a public servant under the IPC and the Prevention of Corruption Act.

A Member of the Appellate Tribunal (PMLA) who leaks confidential case documents to the defence counsel for monetary gain could be prosecuted for breach of trust and misconduct applicable to public servants.

A Deputy Director subordinate to the PMLA Director, while executing a search and seizure operation at a real estate firm in Delhi, carries all the legal protections and obligations of a public servant, ensuring any obstruction of his duties constitutes an offence.

If a clerical employee of the Adjudicating Authority tampers with records related to a money laundering case, they can be prosecuted for offences applicable to public servants such as fabrication of evidence under IPC sections.
what_it_covers: The Chairperson of the Appellate Tribunal constituted under PMLA
Members and employees of the Adjudicating Authority handling attachment and confiscation proceedings
The Director of the Financial Intelligence Unit or the Enforcement Directorate appointed under PMLA
Officers subordinate to the Director, including Joint Directors, Deputy Directors, Assistant Directors, and investigating officers
Other employees and support staff of the Appellate Tribunal and Adjudicating Authority performing official duties under the Act
what_it_excludes: Private lawyers, chartered accountants, or reporting entities such as banks and financial institutions who are not officers of the designated authorities
Witnesses, informants, or persons under investigation who interact with these authorities but hold no official position under the Act

definitions.definition: 'Schedule' means the Schedule to this Act, which contains the list of offences categorised under Part A and Part B, the commission of which, when proceeds are derived therefrom, constitutes the predicate offence for money-laundering under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.
definitions.plain_english: The 'Schedule' is a list appended to the Prevention of Money Laundering Act that enumerates specific crimes (called scheduled offences) whose illegal proceeds can attract money-laundering charges. It is divided into Part A (serious offences tried without a minimum value threshold) and Part B (offences that qualify only if the total value involved is thirty lakh rupees or more). Essentially, if a crime is not listed in the Schedule, money earned from it cannot be prosecuted as money-laundering under this Act.
real_world_examples: A drug trafficker in Mumbai earns crores from narcotics trading; since drug offences under the NDPS Act are listed in Part A of the Schedule, the Enforcement Directorate can attach his properties under PMLA without any minimum value requirement.

A corporate fraudster in Delhi siphons ₹25 lakh through cheque dishonour and cheating offences listed in Part B of the Schedule; since the value is less than ₹30 lakh, these Part B offences do not qualify as scheduled offences, and PMLA prosecution cannot be initiated.

An accused in a Kolkata hawala case is charged with offences under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, which figure in the Schedule; the ED invokes PMLA provisions to search his premises under Section 17 and arrest him under Section 19.

A Hyderabad builder is accused of offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act, which are scheduled offences under Part A; the Special Court takes cognisance under Section 45 of PMLA, and the court applies the twin bail conditions precisely because the predicate offence is listed in the Schedule.

A Bengaluru cybercrime syndicate commits online fraud; since cyber-crime offences under the IT Act are included in the Schedule, proceeds recovered from their bank accounts are treated as 'proceeds of crime' and are liable for attachment and confiscation under PMLA.

definitions.plain_english: A 'scheduled offence' is a predicate crime listed in the Schedule attached to the Prevention of Money Laundering Act. Crimes listed in Part A qualify as scheduled offences regardless of the amount of money involved. Crimes in Part B only qualify if the total money involved is at least thirty lakh rupees (₹30,00,000). Money laundering under PMLA can only be prosecuted if the money was generated from one of these listed scheduled offences.
real_world_examples: A drug trafficking gang in Mumbai generates crores in cash by selling narcotics — drug trafficking is listed in Part A of the Schedule, so it qualifies as a scheduled offence regardless of the amount, enabling the Enforcement Directorate to investigate money laundering.

A politician in Delhi is found to have received illegal gratification of ₹5 lakh under the Prevention of Corruption Act — since the offence falls under Part B and the amount is below ₹30 lakh, it may not constitute a 'scheduled offence', potentially limiting PMLA action.

A fraudster in Hyderabad runs a Ponzi scheme defrauding investors of ₹50 crore — cheating under the Indian Penal Code is a Part B offence, but since the value far exceeds ₹30 lakh, it qualifies as a scheduled offence, triggering PMLA attachment powers.

A terrorist financing network in Jammu & Kashmir channels funds through hawala transactions — offences under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act are listed in Part A, making them scheduled offences irrespective of value, allowing immediate attachment of proceeds.

A customs official in Chennai is caught smuggling luxury goods worth ₹2 crore — offences under the Customs Act are listed in the Schedule, qualifying as a scheduled offence and enabling the ED to investigate and attach proceeds of the smuggling operation.

A corporate executive in Bengaluru manipulates share prices causing losses of ₹40 lakh to investors — securities fraud listed under Part B qualifies as a scheduled offence since the value exceeds ₹30 lakh, permitting PMLA prosecution alongside SEBI action.

Offences under special statutes like the Customs Act, Companies Act, Corruption Act, or SEBI Act that are specifically enumerated in the Schedule and satisfy the applicable value threshold.

what_it_excludes: Offences listed under Part B of the Schedule where the total value involved is less than thirty lakh rupees — such offences fall outside the definition and cannot form the predicate for a PMLA prosecution.

Civil wrongs, regulatory contraventions, or tax defaults that are not specifically listed as offences in the Schedule, even if they result in financial gains to the accused.
Offences that may have been deleted or removed from the Schedule by subsequent amendment, which lose their status as scheduled offences prospectively and cannot ground new PMLA proceedings.

definitions.definition: A 'search' under the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act refers to the authorised physical examination of any building, place, vessel, vehicle, aircraft, or person, conducted by a duly authorised officer who has reason to believe (recorded in writing) that such building, place, or person harbours proceeds of crime, records relating to money-laundering, or evidence connected with an offence under the Act. It encompasses entry into premises, breaking open of locked receptacles, examination of persons on oath, and seizure of records or property found therein, subject to the procedural safeguards prescribed under Sections 17 and 18.
definitions.plain_english: A 'search' means the official inspection carried out by a government officer who has written reasons to believe that a place or a person is hiding money or documents linked to money-laundering. The officer can enter buildings, open locked safes or boxes, look through vehicles or vessels, and check a person's belongings or body for hidden records or illegally obtained money.
