definitions.definition: 'Special Court' means a Court of Session designated as Special Court under sub-section (1) of section 43.
definitions.plain_english: A Special Court is a regular Sessions Court that has been officially designated by the Central Government, in consultation with the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court, to exclusively handle cases under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act. It has the power to try money laundering offences and related matters such as bail applications and appeals. This designation ensures that complex financial crime cases are heard by courts specifically earmarked for this purpose.
real_world_examples: The Sessions Court in Mumbai designated as a Special Court under PMLA hears the trial of a real estate developer accused of layering black money through shell companies registered in multiple states.

A Special Court in Delhi takes cognizance of a chargesheet filed by the Enforcement Directorate against a former bank official alleged to have laundered funds obtained through fraudulent loan disbursements.

The designated Special Court in Chennai adjudicates a bail application filed by an accused hawala operator arrested under PMLA, applying the twin conditions of bail as mandated under section 45 of the Act.

A Special Court in Kolkata tries a case where proceeds of crime derived from drug trafficking were invested in hospitality businesses, with the court overseeing confiscation proceedings alongside the criminal trial.

The Special Court in Hyderabad entertains an appeal against an order of the Adjudicating Authority relating to attachment of properties worth several crore rupees allegedly linked to a chit fund fraud.

A designated Special Court in Ahmedabad conducts trial against accused persons charged with money laundering arising from GST fraud, coordinating with parallel proceedings before the Adjudicating Authority.
what_it_covers: A Court of Session formally designated by the Central Government under section 43(1) of PMLA to try offences of money laundering.
Jurisdiction to take cognizance of offences under PMLA on a complaint filed by the Director or any officer authorised by the Central Government.
Power to try an accused for the scheduled offence as well as for the offence of money laundering where such scheduled offence and the money laundering offence are tried jointly.
Authority to hear and decide bail applications under section 45, applying the twin conditions prescribed therein.
Jurisdiction to issue summons, conduct trials, and pass orders relating to attachment, confiscation, and disposal of proceeds of crime under the Act.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary Sessions Courts that have not been specifically designated under section 43(1) of PMLA — such courts lack jurisdiction over PMLA offences.
The Adjudicating Authority constituted under section 6, which is a civil-administrative body handling attachment and confiscation proceedings and is not a Special Court.
The Appellate Tribunal established under section 25, which is a separate quasi-judicial appellate body and not a Special Court under section 43.
Magistrate courts, Chief Judicial Magistrate courts, or any court below the rank of a Sessions Court, which have no jurisdiction to try PMLA offences.
High Courts and the Supreme Court, which exercise appellate and supervisory jurisdiction but are not designated Special Courts under section 43(1).
definitions.why_it_matters: The designation of a court as a Special Court is the foundational jurisdictional requirement for initiating and conducting a criminal trial under PMLA — without this designation, no court can take cognizance of or try an offence of money laundering under section 44. It also determines which court applies the stringent twin bail conditions under section 45, which directly affects whether an accused can be granted bail pending trial.

definitions.definition: A summons, under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, is a formal legal process issued by the Adjudicating Authority, the Director, or a Special Court requiring a person to appear before such authority or court, whether to give evidence, produce documents or records, or to attend as an accused, during the course of any investigation, proceeding, or trial under the Act. Such summons may also be transmitted to or received from a contracting State for service or execution in cross-border money laundering matters.
definitions.plain_english: A summons is an official written order that tells a person they must appear before an authority — like the Enforcement Directorate, the Adjudicating Authority, or a Special Court — at a specific time and place. It can require the person to come and answer questions, bring documents, or appear as an accused in a money laundering case. Ignoring a summons can lead to serious legal consequences, including criminal liability. Summons can also be sent to or received from foreign countries in international money laundering investigations.
real_world_examples: The Enforcement Directorate issues a summons to the CEO of a Mumbai-based shell company under Section 50, requiring him to appear at the ED's zonal office in Mumbai and produce the company's bank account statements and transaction records suspected to be linked to proceeds of crime.

A Special Court in Delhi issues a summons to an accused money laundering offender who has fled to a contracting State (e.g., the UK), transmitting it in duplicate through the Central Government to the appropriate court in that State for execution under Section 59.

The Adjudicating Authority issues a summons under Section 11 to the compliance officer of a private bank to attend proceedings and give evidence regarding suspicious transactions flagged in a money laundering adjudication matter involving a prominent real estate developer.

A Deputy Director of the Enforcement Directorate, investigating a hawala network operating across Gujarat and Maharashtra, issues summons to multiple money changers requiring them to appear personally and produce their ledgers, cash books, and customer records under Section 50.

A Special Court in Chennai receives a summons issued by a court in a contracting State requiring a key witness residing in India to attend and produce documents related to an international money laundering syndicate, and causes the same to be served locally under Section 59.

In a Ponzi scheme investigation, the Additional Director of the ED issues summons to the chartered accountant and auditor of the accused firm to appear before the investigating officer and state the truth regarding the financial structuring of the scheme.
what_it_covers: A summons issued by the Director, Additional Director, Joint Director, Deputy Director, or Assistant Director under Section 50 to any person whose attendance is necessary for giving evidence or producing records during investigation or proceedings.

A summons issued by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 11 to enforce attendance of any person, including officers of banking companies or financial institutions, for examination on oath during adjudication proceedings.

A summons issued by a Special Court under Section 59 to an accused person or a witness requiring attendance and production of documents, which can be transmitted to a contracting State for service or execution.
A summons received by the Central Government or Special Court from a contracting State under Section 61 for service or execution within Indian jurisdiction in a mutual legal assistance matter.
A summons requiring a person to produce specific records, documents, or other things before the investigating authority or the Special Court in the course of money laundering proceedings.
what_it_excludes: Informal notices or letters issued by the Enforcement Directorate requesting voluntary cooperation or information, which do not carry the binding legal force of a formal summons under Section 50.
A warrant for the arrest of an accused person, which is a distinct legal instrument from a summons and carries different procedural consequences, including physical detention.
Search warrants issued under Section 17 of the Act, which authorise entry and search of premises, as opposed to a summons which commands personal appearance or document production.
Orders of attachment or confiscation, which are substantive enforcement actions against property and are not forms of summons compelling personal attendance.

Communications or requests exchanged between competent authorities that do not constitute a formal judicially or administratively issued command to appear, such as inter-agency information sharing requests.
definitions.why_it_matters: Compliance with a summons under the PMLA is mandatory — persons summoned are legally bound to attend and state the truth, and failure to comply or giving false information exposes them to prosecution for false evidence under Section 193 and Section 228 of the Indian Penal Code, as proceedings are deemed judicial proceedings. The summons power is central to the ED's investigative arsenal, enabling it to compel testimony and document production that can establish the trail of proceeds of crime and trigger attachment, confiscation, or prosecution under Section 3 and Section 4 of the Act.

definitions.definition: A 'survey' means the exercise of power under Section 16 of the Act, whereby an authority, having reason to believe that an offence under Section 3 has been committed, enters any place where the act constituting such offence is carried on, to inspect records, check or verify proceeds of crime or related transactions, and collect information relevant to proceedings under the Act, without effecting a search or seizure of property.
definitions.plain_english: A 'survey' is a formal inspection visit by a government authority (such as a Director or authorised officer under PMLA) to a business premises or any relevant place, to look at records, verify transactions, and gather information about possible money laundering. Unlike a search, a survey does not involve forcible entry or seizure of documents or property. The authority can examine records, make copies, verify proceeds of crime, and record statements of persons present at the place.
real_world_examples: An Enforcement Directorate officer visits a hawala operator's shop in Mumbai, having reason to believe money laundering is occurring there, and inspects the cash ledgers, account books, and transaction records on the premises without seizing them.

An authority conducts a survey of a real estate developer's office in Delhi where suspicious property transactions are being routed, examining sale deeds, bank transfer records, and receipts to verify whether proceeds of crime are involved.

During a survey of a jewellery firm in Chennai suspected of layering black money through gold purchases, the officer records the statement of the accountant present and makes copies of invoices and purchase records.

An PMLA authority surveys a money transfer service business in Hyderabad, inspects its transaction logs and customer KYC files, and prepares an inventory of suspicious remittance transactions linked to a scheduled offence.

Following intelligence inputs, a survey is conducted at a chit fund company's registered office in Kolkata to inspect its subscriber records and cash flow statements to check for possible placement of proceeds of crime.

An authority surveys a hotel in Goa suspected of being used to channel crime proceeds through inflated room bookings, inspecting guest registers, billing records, and bank statements without physically seizing any documents.
what_it_covers: Entry by an authorised PMLA authority into any place where an act constituting a money laundering offence is being carried on, within the area assigned to or authorised for that authority.
Inspection, copying, and marking of records found at the surveyed premises, including financial statements, ledgers, transaction receipts, and electronic records.
Verification and inventory-making of proceeds of crime or transactions related to proceeds of crime found at the place during the survey.
Recording of statements of any proprietor, employee, or other person present and attending to or helping in the suspected activity.
Places where the person carrying on the activity states that records or property relating to the act are kept, even if no activity is visibly conducted at that second location.
what_it_excludes: Forcible search of a building or place involving breaking open locks or sealed receptacles, which falls under the separate power of search under Section 17.
Seizure and physical removal of records, documents, or property from the premises, which is not authorised under a survey but requires a search under Section 17.
Examination of persons on oath, which is a power specifically available during a search under Section 17 but not expressly conferred during a survey under Section 16.

Entry into a place purely on suspicion without recorded reasons — a survey requires the authority to have reason to believe an offence under Section 3 has been committed and to record those reasons in writing.
Actions by persons or officers who are not 'authorities' as designated under the Act; private parties or non-designated officials cannot conduct a survey.
Attachment or confiscation of property found during the survey, as these are distinct consequential powers governed by separate provisions of the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The finding of records or property during a survey triggers the statutory presumption under Section 22 that such records or property belong to the person in whose possession they are found, their contents are true, and signatures are genuine — significantly shifting the evidentiary burden in proceedings under the Act. Whether an inspection qualifies as a 'survey' under Section 16 determines which procedural safeguards apply, what powers the authority lawfully holds on those premises, and whether evidence gathered is admissible in adjudication or prosecution for the offence of money laundering.

definitions.definition: "Tracing" means determining the nature, source, disposition, movement, title or ownership of property.
definitions.plain_english: Tracing means the process of following and figuring out everything about a piece of property — where it came from, who owns it, how it moved, and what happened to it. It is essentially detective work on assets to find out if they are linked to money laundering or a crime. Under this law, authorities use tracing to locate and identify property that may be the proceeds of a crime, even when it has been moved across borders or disguised through complex transactions.
real_world_examples: The Enforcement Directorate traces funds deposited in a Swiss bank account back to a hawala network in Mumbai that originally received money from drug trafficking proceeds, establishing a chain from the criminal source to the foreign asset.

An authority under PMLA traces how a Bengaluru-based politician converted proceeds from a corruption scandal into benami real estate spread across multiple shell companies in Delhi, Goa, and Hyderabad, mapping the full chain of ownership and transfer.

Following a letter of request from a contracting State, the Director directs Indian authorities to trace the movement of funds that were remitted from a Dubai-based fraudster to several Indian bank accounts and then converted into gold jewellery and luxury vehicles.

The Enforcement Directorate traces cryptocurrency holdings back to a Ponzi scheme operator in Kolkata by tracking blockchain wallet addresses, exchange records, and KYC data to establish the source and current disposition of the digital assets.

In a bank loan fraud case involving a major NBFC in Chennai, authorities trace the diversion of sanctioned loan amounts through a web of fictitious invoices and inter-company transfers to offshore accounts in the Cayman Islands, identifying the current title holders of the parked funds.
what_it_covers: Determining the original source of funds or property alleged to be proceeds of crime under section 3 of PMLA.
Establishing the chain of title and successive ownership of property that has been transferred through multiple persons or entities to disguise its criminal origin.
Tracking the physical or financial movement of property, including cross-border transfers, across bank accounts, shell companies, or asset classes such as real estate, gold, or cryptocurrency.
Ascertaining the nature and current disposition of property, including whether it has been converted, commingled, or reinvested in another form after being derived from an offence.
Identifying who holds legal or beneficial title to property suspected to be in a contracting State, pursuant to a letter of request received or issued under Chapter IX of PMLA.
what_it_excludes: Formal arrest or prosecution of individuals — tracing is an investigative function related to property, not a process for establishing personal criminal liability.
Seizure, attachment, or confiscation of property, which are distinct legal actions that may follow tracing but are not part of the definition itself.
Proving that a specific offence under section 3 was committed, which falls under 'identifying' as separately defined in section 55, not under tracing.
Routine banking or financial audits conducted by regulatory bodies such as RBI or SEBI in their supervisory capacity, which are not exercises of the tracing power under PMLA.
Property that has no connection to a scheduled offence or money laundering, as tracing under PMLA is specifically directed at property suspected to be proceeds of crime.

Whether 'tracing' has been properly conducted determines whether a letter of request from or to a contracting State results in actionable enforcement, directly affecting whether proceeds of crime are recovered or remain shielded.
definitions.retrieval_text:
tracing: Tracing means the process of following and figuring out everything about a piece of property — where it came from, who owns it, how it moved, and what happened to it. It is essentially detective work on assets to find out if they are linked to money laundering or a crime. Under this law, authorities use tracing to locate and identify property that may be the proceeds of a crime, even when it has been moved across borders or disguised through complex transactions.

Legal text: "Tracing" means determining the nature, source, disposition, movement, title or ownership of property.

Examples: The Enforcement Directorate traces funds deposited in a Swiss bank account back to a hawala network in Mumbai that originally received money from drug trafficking proceeds, establishing a chain from the criminal source to the foreign asset. | An authority under PMLA traces how a Bengaluru-based politician converted proceeds from a corruption scandal into benami real estate spread across multiple shell companies in Delhi, Goa, and Hyderabad, mapping the full chain of ownership and transfer. | Following a letter of request from a contracting State, the Director directs Indian authorities to trace the movement of funds that were remitted from a Dubai-based fraudster to several Indian bank accounts and then converted into gold jewellery and luxury vehicles. | The Enforcement Directorate traces cryptocurrency holdings back to a Ponzi scheme operator in Kolkata by tracking blockchain wallet addresses, exchange records, and KYC data to establish the source and current disposition of the digital assets. | In a bank loan fraud case involving a major NBFC in Chennai, authorities trace the diversion of sanctioned loan amounts through a web of fictitious invoices and inter-company transfers to offshore accounts in the Cayman Islands, identifying the current title holders of the parked funds.

definitions.definition: 'transfer' includes sale, purchase, mortgage, pledge, gift, loan or any other form of transfer of right, title, possession or lien.
definitions.plain_english: A 'transfer' under this law means any way in which ownership, possession, or rights over a property change hands from one person to another. This includes not just outright selling or buying, but also mortgaging, pledging as security, gifting, or lending property. The definition is very wide and covers virtually any arrangement through which control or interest in a property moves from one party to another.
real_world_examples: A Delhi-based accused in a fraud case sells his residential flat in Noida to a relative for below-market value to move proceeds of crime out of his name — this sale constitutes a 'transfer' under PMLA.
A Mumbai businessman pledges shares (acquired through hawala transactions) with a private lender as collateral for a loan — the act of pledging amounts to a 'transfer' of a lien over those shares.

A Bengaluru-based shell company gifts a commercial property (purchased with laundered funds) to a trust controlled by the accused's family — the gift deed executes a 'transfer' attracting PMLA scrutiny.
A Chennai trader mortgages agricultural land (representing proceeds of crime) to a cooperative bank to obtain working capital — the mortgage is treated as a 'transfer' of rights under PMLA.

A Kolkata-based accused takes a loan against fixed deposits that were funded through scheduled offence proceeds and grants the bank a lien — this creation of a lien qualifies as a 'transfer' under the Act.

A Hyderabad real estate developer purchases multiple flats using proceeds of crime routed through fictitious invoices — the purchase transactions themselves are 'transfers' of title triggering PMLA provisions.
what_it_covers: Sale of immovable or movable property where title passes from the accused to a third party, even at undervalued consideration.
Mortgage of property (movable or immovable) where the mortgagee obtains an interest or lien as security for a debt.
Pledge of movable assets such as jewellery, shares, or fixed deposit receipts to secure a loan, creating a possessory interest in the pledgee.
Gift of property — including benami transfers — where the accused gratuitously transfers title or possession to a family member or associate.
Loan of property where temporary possession or use rights are transferred to another person.
Any other arrangement — such as assignment, lease, or hypothecation — that results in transfer of any right, title, possession, or lien over property.
what_it_excludes: Mere change in market value of property without any act of transfer of right, title, possession, or lien — passive appreciation or depreciation does not constitute a transfer.
Court-ordered attachment itself, which is specifically defined separately as a 'prohibition' of transfer under the definition of 'attachment' in Section 2, not a transfer.
Internal accounting entries or book adjustments within the same legal entity that do not result in any actual movement of right, title, possession, or lien over property to another person.
Destruction or consumption of property, which extinguishes rights rather than transferring them to another party.
Inheritance or succession by operation of law upon death of the accused, which occurs automatically and not through a voluntary act of transfer.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a transaction qualifies as a 'transfer' determines whether it can be prohibited under the attachment provisions of Chapter III and whether it constitutes a step in the process of money-laundering under Section 3; if a transaction is a 'transfer', authorities can provisionally attach the property under Section 5 and the accused may face prosecution for concealing or dealing with proceeds of crime.

definitions.definition: Untainted property is not formally defined in the Act, but is used in contradistinction to 'proceeds of crime': it refers to any property that has no connection, direct or indirect, to a scheduled offence and has been acquired through legitimate, lawful means. Under Section 3, the offence of money-laundering is constituted by projecting proceeds of crime as untainted property, and under Section 24, the burden of proving that proceeds of crime are untainted property lies on the accused.
definitions.plain_english: Untainted property is property that is genuinely clean — it has been earned or acquired through legal means and has no link to any crime. It is the opposite of 'proceeds of crime', which is money or assets derived from criminal activity. In a money-laundering case, if you are accused, you must prove to the court that your property is untainted, meaning it came from a legitimate source.
real_world_examples: A salaried software engineer in Bengaluru purchases a flat using savings from his salary and a home loan from a nationalised bank. This flat qualifies as untainted property because its source is entirely lawful employment income with no nexus to any scheduled offence.

A farmer in Punjab sells agricultural land inherited from his father and deposits the proceeds in a bank account. Those funds are untainted property since the transaction originates from a legitimate inheritance and legal sale, not from any criminal activity.

A Mumbai-based businessman accused under PMLA demonstrates through audited balance sheets, income tax returns, and bank statements that the amount in his account represents revenue from his garment export business duly reported to tax authorities, thereby establishing the funds as untainted property.

A Kolkata jeweller, whose accounts are attached by the Enforcement Directorate, produces GST invoices, purchase bills from registered suppliers, and bank transfer records to show that the gold stock was purchased from legitimate trade channels, seeking to establish it as untainted property before the Adjudicating Authority.

An NRI returning to India transfers foreign earnings from a documented employment in the UAE into an Indian bank account. When questioned, he produces foreign employment contracts, salary slips, and RBI-compliant remittance records to prove the funds are untainted property with no connection to any scheduled offence.
what_it_covers: Property acquired exclusively through lawful income such as salary, business profits, agricultural earnings, or inheritance that is properly documented and has no link to any scheduled offence.
Assets purchased using funds that can be traced to legitimate, tax-compliant sources, such as savings deposits, bank loans, or legally earned investment returns.
Funds remitted by Non-Resident Indians from verifiable foreign employment or business earnings that have no connection to any crime listed in the Schedule to the PMLA.
Property received as a gift or bequest from a family member where the donor's source of funds is itself clean and unconnected to any criminal activity.
what_it_excludes: Any property that constitutes 'proceeds of crime', i.e., property derived or obtained, directly or indirectly, from any person as a result of criminal activity relating to a scheduled offence.
Assets that have been commingled with proceeds of crime, even if a portion of the funds used for acquisition was legitimate, where the criminal-origin taint cannot be separated.
Property in respect of which the accused fails to discharge the reverse burden of proof under Section 24 — such property cannot be treated as untainted regardless of the accused's claim.

Assets acquired through transactions that are structurally designed to disguise the criminal origin of funds, such as layered transfers through shell companies, even if the end-asset appears clean on its face.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether property qualifies as untainted determines the very commission of the offence under Section 3 — projecting proceeds of crime as untainted property is the core act of money-laundering, attracting prosecution, attachment, and confiscation. Under Section 24, an accused bears the reverse burden of proving their property is untainted, meaning failure to discharge this burden can result in conviction and loss of the property.

definitions.definition: 'Value' means the fair market value of any property on the date of its acquisition by any person, or if such date cannot be determined, the date on which such property is possessed by such person.
definitions.plain_english: Value refers to the fair market price of a property at the time it was bought or acquired by a person. If the exact date of acquisition cannot be pinned down, the law uses the date when the person first came into possession of the property. This helps authorities calculate how much money was involved in suspected money laundering activities.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based businessman acquires a residential flat in Pune worth ₹1.5 crore using proceeds of crime in 2019; the 'value' of that property for PMLA purposes is ₹1.5 crore, its fair market value on the date of acquisition in 2019.

A hawala operator in Delhi receives gold bullion whose purchase date is untraceable; authorities determine 'value' based on the fair market price of the gold on the date the operator was found to be in possession of it.

A politician in Hyderabad acquires agricultural land through benami transactions where the registration date is disputed; enforcement officers use the date of actual possession to ascertain the fair market value for computing proceeds of crime.

A company in Chennai purchases commercial machinery worth ₹80 lakh using funds linked to a scheduled offence in 2021; the 'value' is assessed at ₹80 lakh (fair market value on the acquisition date) for determining whether the Part B Schedule threshold of ₹30 lakh is met.

An accused in a drug trafficking case in Kolkata holds foreign currency that cannot be traced to a specific acquisition date; the Enforcement Directorate treats the date of seizure as the possession date and calculates its rupee fair market value on that date for attachment proceedings.
what_it_covers: Fair market value of immovable property such as land or buildings on the date of their acquisition by the accused person.
Fair market value of movable assets such as gold, jewellery, vehicles, or foreign currency on the date of acquisition or, if unknown, on the date of possession.
Fair market value of intangible assets such as shares, securities, or intellectual property rights on the date they were acquired or possessed by the person.
Situations where the acquisition date is undetermined, in which case the fair market value is assessed as of the date the property was found to be possessed by the person.
Valuation of property for computing whether the total value of a Part B Schedule offence meets the ₹30 lakh threshold.
what_it_excludes: Subjective or book value of property — the definition mandates fair market value, not purchase price, depreciated cost, or declared value in accounts.
Future projected value or appreciation of property after the date of acquisition or possession, as the definition is anchored to a specific past date.
Value determined by personal or private agreement between parties that does not reflect fair market conditions prevailing on the relevant date.
Notional or imputed value assigned by parties to defeat the provisions of the Act, such as deliberately undervaluing transactions below prescribed thresholds.
Income or revenue generated from the property after acquisition, which would be separately assessed rather than forming part of the 'value' as defined.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'value' is critical because it determines the monetary quantum of 'proceeds of crime,' which directly governs whether an offence qualifies under Part B of the Schedule (requiring a minimum value of ₹30 lakh) and sets the ceiling for attachment, seizure, and confiscation orders under Chapter III of the Act. An incorrect valuation can either exclude a case from PMLA jurisdiction or lead to disproportionate attachment of assets beyond what is legally permissible.
